Minimalist Beach House Doubles as a Frame for the Ocean It Overlooks

Casa Malonic, or Malonic House, is a recently completed residential project in the beach town of Zihuatanejo, Mexico. But this is no ordinary beach house. Instead, it serves the striking oceanic landscape at its feet. Conceived by Mexico-based firm HW Studio , the entire design draws from two defining elements: the land it sits on and its colors, resulting in a construction that engages in a soft yet profound dialogue with the surrounding environment.

This gentle approach is almost a secret, for those who come across Casa Malonic from the street would see only a white mass wrapped in a single curved wall that almost signals brutalism . As the dwellers step inside, the entrance path leads to a circular courtyard where a soothing transition begins, as if the house sheds concrete layers to reveal its true nature. The walls then give way to a boundless view of the ocean and the surrounding landscape.

When first approaching the construction site, the architects were so fascinated by the area that they wanted to spotlight it. They made a point to honor the elements that predated the architecture: flora, fauna, topography, and sunlight. To do that, they reduced architecture to ground, roof, and shadow—its most basic elements. They found inspiration in an enramada , a simple shelter beneath a canopy that, even at its barest, can provide shade and protection from rain without enforcing a strict boundary.

This concept is what creates the most striking feature of Casa Malonic. Rather than providing just another floor-to-ceiling window or glass balcony to take in the beach landscape, the entire structure doubles as a frame for the horizon line. It’s also through this choice that the architects declare this view the spiritual heart of the house. To them, the horizon line is what makes the design possible; not the other way around.

Meant to be taken in as an all-encompassing habitat, the oceanic imagery is not limited to the views. The flooring imitates color and texture, evoking the sand below, as if establishing one continuous path to it. The white walls match the landscape by recalling the flowers of the nine Cacalosúchil trees that surround the house.

“The materiality does not seek to represent the landscape, but to establish a sensory continuity with it. Architecture is first experienced through the feet, before it is understood through the eyes,” writes HW Studio. “The project does not seek to reproduce nature, nor to disappear completely into it. It seeks to construct a precise relationship with the site through a few operations: contain, move through, subtract, and open. The house is ultimately understood as a balance between matter and void.”

Japanese Club Hosts a “Book Rave,” Trading Thumping Beats for Cozy Reading

In Japan, a nightclub traded loud music for books—for a day. A venue named SPREAD , located in Tokyo’s Shimokitazawa district, known for its alternative, bohemian vibes, hosted a “Book Rave.” The club turned the dance floor into a reading lounge with carpets where attendees could sit or lie down to read, as a DJ played ambient music to keep everyone focused. This isn’t a new trend taking over Japanese clubs; instead, it’s a unique event that has caught the world’s attention.

JUCY organized the event , and its Instagram bio simply reads, “We’re hosting Reading Parties at various locations in Tokyo.” The JUCY BOOK RAVE at SPREAD appears to be its first. And while it was held at a nightclub, the so-called “rave” ran from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. on a Saturday.

Instead of bringing their own books, attendees read the title recommended by the JUCY crew. The organizers also had some fiction titles available for sale. Attendees later discussed what they were reading and shared and traded books with others. According to the venue’ s event flyer, the ¥2,500 ($15.80) cover charge included two drinks and a copy of the book they read.

“This event is not a gathering where participants bring their own books to read; rather, it is an event where everyone reads a single work of literary fiction designated by the organizers,” the team said when promoting a second of these getogethers. “The book we plan to read for this event is Kohei Toyonaga’s Tsuki no Hashiri ya, Uma no Hashiri . We do not recommend participation if you have already read this book (though you are more than welcome to join if you’d like to reread it and share your thoughts with other participants.”
If you’re in the Tokyo area, follow JUCY on Instagram to stay up to date on its reading events.

Olivia Mazzola explores beauty, femininity, and the poetry of human emotion through her refined approach to portraiture.
Olivia Mazzola is a member of the Beautiful Bizarre Artist Directory

Olivia Mazzola explores beauty, femininity, and the poetry of human emotion through her refined approach to portraiture. Guided by light as her primary expressive language, she transforms intimate moments into dreamlike imagery where elegance becomes both the subject and the sensation it evokes. Her work invites viewers into a world where vulnerability becomes power, softness reveals its own quiet strength, and emotion is held in its most graceful, luminous form.

In Olivia Mazzola’s photographic style, there is a deliberate tension between stillness and motion, clarity and mystery. In every frame, she searches for the fleeting instant in which the subject becomes more than themselves where elegance slips into the surreal, and the unseen speaks louder than what is visible. Her goal is not to simply document a person, but to invite viewers into a realm of abstraction where femininity is fluid, blurred, timeless, and charged with imagination.

Olivia’s narrative foundation is rooted in the concept of “Eramnesía” , a neologism drawn from Greek that evokes the sensation of having been born in the wrong historical era a nostalgia for a time one has never lived. Photography allows her to build this parallel, imaginary world where her vision is in constant dialogue with the dreamlike and the concealed, with what is quietly revealed in the margins. Her subjects appear to emerge from a suspended moment in time, becoming both present and elusive: a silhouette of longing, a blurred recollection, an icon stripped of narrative certainty.

Motion and darkness lie at the core of Olivia’s language. Blurred atmospheres, dissolving contours, and garments that behave like extensions of the psyche all shape her pursuit of a dreamlike state. Through light-painting, using continuous light and intentional camera movement during long exposures, she generates images that feel at once kinetic and ephemeral. She further deepens this sensorial world through reflections, refractions, and both double and multiple exposures, building layers that echo her fascination with the elusive, the remembered, and the imagined.

Giant Spiral Staircase Roof Leads To Incredible Views at Shanghai’s New Opera House

The Shanghai Grand Opera House , set along the Huangpu River, is more than a place to enjoy cultural performances. The striking building—designed by Norwegian architecture firm Snøhetta —features an epic, spiraling rooftop staircase that invites you to climb toward the clouds and enjoy spectacular views.

Spanning 1,569,991 square feet (146,786 square meters), the Opera House is built around three key ideas: movement, belonging, and experience. The design makes it easy for people to approach, enter, and explore the building, while creating an open, welcoming space for everyone. Every detail is designed with the visitor in mind, from the interior atmosphere to the journey audiences and performers take through the building.

The building’s sculptural form draws on the flow of the Huangpu River and the energy of the surrounding city, with the spiraling roof at its heart. It doubles as a stage, viewing deck, and gathering space that people can enjoy year-round. The huge spiral structure leads from the ground floor to the roof, offering views of the river and city skyline along the way and making the journey itself part of the experience. It also brings together a variety of public spaces, including restaurants, exhibition areas, education centers, and performance halls.

The opera house’s modern exterior reflects the contemporary performances and productions inside. The impressive building features three auditoriums hosting everything from traditional opera and classical music to experimental performances.
Find out more about the Shanghai Grand Opera House design on the Snøhetta website .

What’s creative risk you’ve taken that completely changed your perspective or practice?

My biggest creative risk was also a physical one: deciding to bring my camera and gear on my adventures. Exploring the backcountry with the necessary survival gear is one thing. Adding the weight and bulk of a camera, lenses, batteries, tripod, etc. and committing to long days carrying it all over challenging terrain, is another. It was a creative decision with real consequences for both my artistic practice and my physical body, and it made all the difference in how I see and create images in the wilderness.
If your work could whisper one thing to the viewer, what would it say?
It would whisper what I hear in my own ear when I’m in the flow, making pictures… look for the spark of magic everywhere, and follow it.
In moments of self-doubt or burnout, what do you do to enable to keep going?

Honestly, I usually walk away and give myself time and space to focus on something else I enjoy. I read a good book, hang out with friends, take pictures of something completely different, throw a party, go camping, and so on. I’ve learned that forcing myself to work through true self-doubt or burnout does the exact opposite of what I want. I like to give my brain and creative soul a break, and it always surprises me how quickly things come back together after some fun.
Has envy ever shown up in your creative journey? How have you learned to cope with or transform it?

Probably? I truly love watching my friends succeed, but I’m sure I’ve felt envy at some point. Jealousy is an emotion I find a bit gross, so I try not to entertain it. I guess that if it does start to show its ugly face, I take it as it as a hint about what I want more of in my work, then I quickly get back to minding my own business.

Martin Blanco born 1974 in Buenos Aires, resides in The Principality of Andorra. He is an internationally exhibited and awarded Digital and Traditional Artist with a Bachelor’s Degree in Fine Arts.

Experimenting with different techniques and boundaries, he has created his own style of creative narrative through Digital Art by mixing photographic manipulation and digital painting. In addition to his digital work, Martin is also dedicated to traditional art, creating detailed graphite drawings and oil paintings that explore both classical and contemporary themes. His mastery of these mediums allows him to express a wide range of ideas, from precise realism to imaginative interpretations, further enriching his artistic practice. He has won 30 international awards, of which 10 are first prizes in several Drawing and Digital Art contests worldwide, including the award of “Best Comic Book” in the New York Horror Film Festival 2007.

His work has been the subject of a number of solo exhibitions in Argentina, Spain and Andorra and he has participated in more than 50 group and juried exhibitions, including events in New York, Paris, London, Berlin, Los Angeles, Barcelona, Warsov, Florence, Dublin, among others.

Martin Blanco has been exploring human nature and its weaknesses in the world we live in since 2008. Fears, anguish, anxieties, and everything that conditions us as the mortal beings we are. His work combines the tension between technique, emotion, and the subconscious by mixing the compositional rigor and chiaroscuro of Renaissance and Baroque painting with the conceptual freedom of surrealism, creating atmospheres that oscillate between beauty, density, and introspection. These influences coexist within his compositions, where contrasts of light and darkness not only define space but also mirror the emotional states of his figures.

For Martín, the meaning of an artwork lies beyond beauty itself. Composition, color, and light all serve a narrative function, instruments that translate an inner discourse into visual form. As he notes, “Creating something beautiful is not enough if it lacks meaning; beauty may define things, but it is not necessarily intrinsic.”

His intention is not merely to impress but to connect to invite viewers into a visual conversation that provokes thought and emotion. If the work succeeds in transmitting the essence of what he intended, then that exchange, that moment of reflection, becomes the true reward.

‘The Book of the Human Body’ Surveys 2,000 Years of Remarkable Anatomical Inquiry
We've long wanted to understand our innards.

As long as humans have been around, we’ve been curious about existential questions like, Why are we here? And how do things work? That goes for our own bodies, too. But in our era of modern science and medicine, it’s difficult to imagine a time when physicians weren’t familiar with all of the bones in the skeleton, how a baby grows inside a womb, or how the cardiovascular system works. Even the profession that comes to mind when we think of a doctor didn’t really emerge until the past few centuries. During the medieval period, barber-surgeons were the primary medical practitioners (yes, the people who cut hair also conducted surgeries).

As medicine morphed into a scientific and intellectual pursuit, academies cropped up starting in the late 1700s, such as the College of Philadelphia—the first medical school in the U.S.—and the Edinburgh School of Surgery in Scotland. Ethics were, let’s say, malleable. In Edinburgh, a legal shortage of fresh cadavers used for study in the early 1800s spawned a shady underground trade in bodies, many of which were dug up from new burials in the dead of night. And then there were the famous serial murders committed by William Burke and William Hare, who cashed in by selling well over a dozen of their victims’ corpses to anatomist Robert Knox for use during his lectures. Suffice it to say, some scholars really wanted to understand our innards.

Slated for release in January, The Book of the Human Body delves into the art and science of anatomy, disease, reproduction, and more. Published by TASCHEN, the two-volume set compiles more than 950 images from over 75 rare books and manuscripts from around the world. From ancient analyses to medieval studies to modern diagrams, the anthology surveys the breadth of eras and cultural influences that have shaped our understanding of our physical selves.

Authored by medical historian Richard Barnett, the book celebrates universality and unquenched curiosity. Despite sleeping, breathing, and walking around in our bodies every day, we are often still mystified by much of what makes them work. Throughout history, that sense of wonder has remained constant. Barnett says, “Whatever they might represent, whatever they might express, these extraordinary images have lost none of their power to shock or captivate, to teach or inspire.”

Illustrations include a silk manuscript dated to 168 B.C.E., discovered in a tomb in southern China, which features 44 figures engaged in exercises of “self-cultivation,” plus excerpts from Andreas Vesalius’s anatomical atlas, Fabrica , published in 1543. “In all of these examples, the illustrations stand out not only as objects of medical understanding, but as conspicuous works of art in their own right,” the publisher says.

Dick Raaijmakers and Horst Rickels ~ FORT KLANK
Can a fort be an instrument? In the hands of Dick Raaijmakers, Horst Rickels and Walter Maioli, it can be, and is. Constructed in the 19th century, Fort Asperen has become the “outer shell”…

Can a fort be an instrument? In the hands of Dick Raaijmakers, Horst Rickels and Walter Maioli , it can be, and is. Constructed in the 19th century, Fort Asperen has become the “outer shell” for a series of mechanical installations designed to bring the fort to sonic life. These instruments channel wind, amplify vibrations and create natural percussion, making the fort a living thing: FORT KLANK.

The 24-minute track operates as a virtual tour of the facility. One is free to imagine the fort’s history, from protector of the realm to tourist destination. When a gong is struck, one thinks of kingly processions; vast metallic scrapes come across as anachronistic heaters and boilers, reminders that when the fort was created, steam power was in vogue. Various sounds skitter around the background like wild mice no one has been able to eliminate, while the louder squeaks of doors and creaks of hinges suggest the ghosts of those who may have died there.

A massive blast in the fifth minute comes across as a furnace of sound: a call to arms, perhaps, or the heart of the Industrial Revolution. Were forts always this loud? If so, how did anyone sleep? Today’s unmanned forts could benefit from more such installations, which return a sense of their original mystery. After the blast comes near-silence and a snipping like embroidery; perhaps there were conjugal visits.

Large metallic dragging sounds occupy the center, a reminder of how hard it is to move large machinery. The gong returns before the density increases again. The very presence of a fortress implies the possibility of battle, which seems to break out in the eighteenth minute: all hands on deck! The internal mechanisms are howling, the outer walls are in in danger of being breached, and the cacophony alone is intense enough to strike fear into the hearts of siege makers and those under siege. Watery sounds join the fray, implying boiling, heating and the use of force. Then it is quiet again: the threat has passed, history has left the fort behind, and visitors are free to travel its corridors, wondering at its walls, its foundations, and most of all its sounds, as strange as the passage of time. (Richard Allen)

As Macy's this week celebrates the 100th edition of its Thanksgiving Day Parade , the department store finds itself at a turning point. After years of questionable financial prospects, Macy's is trying to reinvent — as a luxury destination.
The retailer's gambit is to keep its old shoppers while also attracting new customers, who will perhaps pay more for real leather and upscale brands.
How Macy's got squeezed in the middle
Long before the pandemic, Macy's was grappling with America's shrinking middle class — and its own lack of fresh vision.
The department store business, to begin with, has become challenging. Big store space is expensive. Online competition is stiff. Shoppers are increasingly buying directly from their favorite brands.
And Macy's faces its own struggle. The chain is neither a discounter like Kohl's or T.J.Maxx, nor an upscale store like Bergdorf Goodman or Nordstrom. Macy's has languished in between.
Here's how the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade is brought to life

"They were kind of like right in the middle," says Michael Prendergast, who advises retailers and brands at the consulting firm Alvarez & Marsal. "Now over time, that middle tier basically got crushed."
When the pandemic hit, store closures had Macy's forecasting an estimated $1.1 billion in losses. Its stock value dropped so low that the company was kicked off the big-league index, the S&P 500.
At one point, Macy's seemed to throw every other thing on discount just to get people buying something .
A shopper with a bag from rival Target visits Macy's in New York.
Stores looked disheveled and chaotic. Shoppers regularly noted a lack of workers to help on the floor. Over 2023, sales at Macy's dropped almost 7% .
Soaring inflation all but forced Macy's hand.

As the so-called K-shaped economy split the nation in recent years, folks with less money turned to Walmart or Target, which stepped up their game. Wealthier people continued to be the ones doing most of the spending, but also not at Macy's — leaning toward higher-end shops.
"For their size and scale the choice is almost made for them," says Prendergast, who's spent 20 years in the fashion business, including selling to Macy's at Tommy Hilfiger.
"If you're Macy's you say, 'We're still getting squeezed in the middle, our customer base in the U.S. is getting squeezed in the middle. Where can we go?' And really the only answer is to go up."
Luxury is now the big Macy's bet.
The retailer already owns the upscale Bloomingdale's, with its designer brands. Macy's also owns the luxury beauty chain Bluemercury.
In 2024, the head of Bloomingdale's took over the entire Macy's company and announced a turnaround plan, " A Bold New Chapter ."
It included closing 150 stores and upgrading more than 300 others. Changes were proposed for the website and the staffing. Stores began to tackle clutter and add nicer items.
"We needed to remove the duplication, the redundancy," says Julie Walsh, senior vice president at Macy's whose team buys women's accessories and beauty products, including shoes, jewelry and makeup.
"When you come onto our floor now, it's a little bit lighter," she says. "So that the product that is on the floor shows up in a meaningful way."
Putting the higher prices to the test
In March, Macy's finally reported a year of growing sales.
The higher-end Bloomingdale's stores continued to drive much of the company's growth, but changes seemed to start paying off at Macy's, too.
The jewels of Route 66: Neon signs are making a comeback
To commemorate the centennial of the famous highway, cities like Tulsa are investing in an old-fashioned technology.
A neon sign lights up at sunset in Tulsa, Okla.

During its heyday, Route 66 became an iconic road trip, connecting the main streets of cities and small towns from Chicago to Los Angeles. And neon signs were the radiant jewels scattered along the roadside.

The glowing glass lights were a fairly new thing when Route 66 opened in November 1926. Parisian Georges Claude had invented the idea of running electricity through tubing filled with neon gas in 1910. The first neon sign arrived in the U.S. in 1922, at a Packard car dealership, and locals were wonderstruck. Reportedly, gapers caused traffic jams.

Claude sold franchises, including one to what is now Claude Neon Federal Signs, founded 100 years ago, just like Route 66. It's still in operation in Tulsa, and the company's website says it's the largest sign company in Oklahoma.

CNF Signs still has "neon benders" — artisans who heat glass tubes in a fire and bend the glass by hand to form shapes and letters, just as Claude did. One of them is Tom Wolski, who said he tells visitors to his studio to stand way back.
Top: Tom Wolski is one of the two full-time neon benders at CNF Signs in Tulsa. Left: He heats two glass tubes to weld them together for a neon sign. Right: An array of glass tubes for neon signs.

"In this room you have extreme electricity. You have fire, you have phosphorus, you have mercury. It is kind of dangerous; you have to pay attention to what you're doing. God knows why I would want to do this, but I love it," Wolski said, laughing.
He was once one of two full-time neon benders at CNF Signs, but fewer and fewer companies have commissioned them, because they're so expensive.

Instead, many are turning to LEDs, which can seem like neon. LEDS are less expensive to make and operate and are less dangerous. But Joe Kesterson, senior designer at CNF Signs, maintains that LEDs are not as beautiful.
Joe Kesterson looks up at a neon sign at the Route 66 Neon Sign Park during a tour of neon signs in Tulsa.
Neon glows, like a candle, he explained. LED lights are brighter and sharper.
Hop in: We're taking a pop culture road trip on Route 66
It may be easy to mistake LED lights for neon lights, he added, but "once you see both of them together, you can see [the LEDs] have almost a harshness to the light."
An interesting fact: Neon lights themselves are not all neon gas.
"Neon gas is red when it illuminates," Kesterson said. "And so anything that you see that's got a warm color is usually going to have neon in it. But cool colors are made using argon gas."
Neon gas is used in warm colors, but argon gas is used to make cool colors, according to Joe Kesterson, senior designer at CNF Signs.
Plus a couple of beads of mercury, which keeps the gas's molecules unstable and energized.
Route 66 and the quest to connect America
The argon-and-mercury combination interacts with a phosphor powder coating on the inside of some tubes, which makes them glow in a rainbow of colors.

"And it never works like you think it would," Kesterson said. "It's not like we learned in school, where blue and yellow make green. If I put blue gas in a yellow piece of neon, a lot of times it's orange or some weird color that you would not expect."
A neon sign beckons visitors to stay at the Desert Hills Motel along Route 66 in Tulsa.
Those bright colors "are part of the mystique of Route 66," Kesterson said. "That's what you would have seen traveling as a child with your parents across the country."

Born Erased ~ What You Destroy, I Love
Born Erased brings together two sides of Bulgarian musician Angel Simitchiev’s musical practice: the dark ambient experimentation of his former solo project Mytrip and the harsher sounds of…

Born Erased brings together two sides of Bulgarian musician Angel Simitchiev’s musical practice: the dark ambient experimentation of his former solo project Mytrip and the harsher sounds of Dayin, which he once described as “Harsh drones and regret. But it’s a relief.” His third outing as Born Erased, What You Destroy, I Love , revisits the concrete angst of his 2023 debut, I Am the End of the World , with a heavier emphasis on guitars and live percussion. There’s even a touch of colour, at least in Silvana Ilieva’s artwork, which resembles molten lava flowing beneath the earth’s surface.

Simitchiev, however, offers no soothing remedy for the world’s ailments. Written in response to the seemingly endless cycle of wars, human suffering and environmental destruction, the album is an expression of anger at humanity’s willingness to sacrifice life and the natural world in pursuit of power and profit. The opening “Knife Hands” establishes the mood with crushing drones that ebb and flow beneath skies already blackened by an unrelenting darkness, like ink rapidly spreading across watercolour paper. “Sea of Skin” begins with a low rumble from the earth’s core before erupting into post-rock territory, propelled by drums and distorted guitars.

As Simitchiev explains in the accompanying interview, the compositions began as ambient pieces, with drummer Nedislav Miladinov invited to respond freely to their atmosphere. Only afterwards did Simitchiev write the guitar and bass parts around the recorded drums. This approach accounts for some of the music’s unpredictable momentum, as the pieces expand and contract under their own considerable weight.

On “Diamond Silence”, the magmatic force reaches the surface, accompanied by the ghostly vocals of Romain Barbot of Saåad, whose fragile presence offers a rare moment of intimacy. “Like Wraiths” takes us across scorched earth, while “The Last Embrace” moves through coruscating textures, with Siavash Amini contributing additional layers of noise and disquiet.

“Unbelonging” retreats into more familiar dark ambient territory, its steady drumming offering a deceptive sense of reassurance as sweeping, glacial drones clear the horizon of any remaining sonic debris. The piece eventually erupts into a volcanic torrent of distortion, dispelling any illusion of safety. It’s this false familiarity that makes the album so unsettling: just when the music seems to offer some respite, the ground gives way again.

The closing “A Future Without the Body” abandons all hope of salvation. Its thrusting, strident passages seem intent on stripping away the last remnants of humanity before gradually dissipating into thin air. The silence left in their wake is all the more powerful.

What You Destroy, I Love offers little prospect of redemption. Simitchiev’s anger is directed not at the natural world but at humanity’s determination to destroy it, along with itself. If there is any hope remaining, it lies in the possibility that the planet might eventually reclaim what we have so recklessly squandered.
Born Erased live by Niya Kirkova
To uncover the different layers of the production process I have reached out directly to Angel Simitchiev .

What You Destroy, I Love sounds considerably heavier than Birds Drink My Blood , with elements of shoegaze and post-rock. In some ways, it feels closer to your debut, I Am the End of the World , which drew on your background in hardcore punk. Was this a conscious return to that sound? And how much did Nedislav Miladinov’s drumming influence the direction of the album?

The new record is certainly heavier and closer to the music of the debut full-length; it was actually written and recorded right after I released I Am the End of the World . However, the production took longer than I expected for multiple reasons, and while waiting for everything to be ready – meaning guest features, mixing, mastering, artwork – I took a little detour from this heavier, guitar- and live drums-oriented sound and made Birds Drink My Blood , which sounds closer to what I was doing with my previous, and now defunct, solo project Mytrip or what I’ve been releasing under the name Dayin .

The “Amphibian Modernist” Who Refused to Imitate
A giant of the Latin American avant-garde, Venezuelan artist Oswaldo Vigas helped define a modernism that resisted Eurocentric ideals.

GUANGZHOU, China — In a June 1985 article in the Venezuelan newspaper El Nacional , painter Oswaldo Vigas decried the exhibition Rauschenberg and the Third World , a traveling show organized by the Rauschenberg Overseas Culture Interchange (ROCI) program at Museo de Arte Contemporáneo de Caracas. “Latin America, both in its literature and in its visual arts, has always been characterized by possessing its own languages, through which it expresses conceptions of the world and of humanity that have nothing to envy in those developed by those other societies,” the late Venezuelan artist wrote of Robert Rauschenberg’s paternalistic Cold War initiative. “If there is anything important I see in this exhibition … it is its value as an example of precisely what we Latin Americans neither should nor have any reason to imitate.”

A giant of the Latin American avant-garde who worked between his home country and Paris, Vigas, who died in 2014, helped define a modernism that resisted Eurocentric ideals. Instead, he favored experimentation that reflected Venezuela’s Indigenous past and a hopeful vision for the future. This struggle — and fusion — between aesthetics and culture is at the center of the Guangdong Museum of Art’s survey of the artist’s work, Reality Is What I Imagine .

The space started as Galleri Faurschou in Copenhagen in 1986 and later expanded to Beijing. The New York outpost was opened in 2019, hosting exhibitions including Ai Weiwei's What You See Is What You See , a 2024 show that Hyperallergic 's co-founder and editor-at-large Hrag Vartanian said pushed viewers “to assert our own agency in our interpretations.”

Unmaking the World With Jack Halberstam
The gender theorist’s latest book charts a constellation of artworks, critical theory, and science-fiction “unworlds,” particularly in the work of artist Gordon Matta-Clark and queer…

For decades, Jack Halberstam has been extolling the virtues of not doing what we’re supposed to — or not doing anything at all. In 2011’s The Queer Art of Failure , for instance, the pioneering gender and queer theorist posited failing as a form of creative resistance to capitalist concepts of success; in 2020’s Wild Things: The Disorder of Desire , he suggested “wildness” as a force of queer disruption to the status quo; and in 1998’s seminal Female Masculinity , he reimagined masculinity severed from maleness. His latest book, Anarchitecture After Everything: A Trans Manifesto (2026), treads further still into the terrain of queer opposition with a philosophy of unmaking and reorganizing the built environment, which he calls “unworlding,” in order to dismantle heteronormative social structures.

In contrast to “world-building,” which seeks to enact change within the parameters of these systems, Halberstam explains that “an unworld is not simply the opposite of the world we inhabit … An unworld must also unthink the logics of this world that make contemporary life under capitalism seem inevitable and right.”

The book’s thesis is summarized in its first sentence: “Anarchitecture, a set of art practices that emerged in the 1970s out of experiments with the sculpting of abandoned buildings, offers an expansive language for thinking about how bodies (and specifically trans bodies) emerge as a consequence of cutting, breaking, dismantling, and collapse.” Since space and bodies organize our daily lives and larger economic and sociopolitical sphere, “cutting” them isn’t just a symbolic act; as Halberstam writes, it’s about making “strategic cuts into the support system for our unfriendly climate and our racist world.”

Unknown Audio Device is an album ensconced in a bootable, browser-based digital art project from an anonymous Parisian musician-programmer who goes by UAD. Presenting music as an isolated…

Unknown Audio Device is an album ensconced in a bootable, browser-based digital art project from an anonymous Parisian musician-programmer who goes by UAD . Presenting music as an isolated, integrated art-object that demands focused attention is admirable and is to move against the current. In the 1970s, cultural theorist Raymond Williams developed the concept ‘flow’ to better describe television, a medium that, rather than being separated into discreet units separated in time and space like film or theater, is an undifferentiated broadcast sequence that can be shut on and off like a tap.

This distinction describes today’s media ecosystem fairly well, one defined by algorithmically-steered, demographically-targeted autoplay, advertising bombardment, and the endless scroll. Renewed interest in physical media: Polaroid photography, vinyl records, paper journaling, and boutique Blu-rays can be interpreted as a gesture against this, however deliberate, alongside multimedia projects like Unknown Audio Device .

Unfortunately, it is one of those projects where the concept at the aforementioned level of abstraction is better than the execution. The aesthetic is tired. Poison-green phosphor CRT as a cyberfictional architectural gesture has been present in fiction at least since William Gibson’s 1982 novella Burning Chrome and trendy at least since The Matrix . Fitting the visual aesthetic to electronic music was, in turn, pre-empted well over a decade ago by vaporwave microgenres like outrun and video games like Geometry Dash (while this reviewer admittedly could not find the ‘mini-games’ mentioned on the project’s itch page , they are probably less enjoyable). Meanwhile, these sort of multimedia musical web projects have existed for over two decades in less austere, more visually inventive forms . To top it off, the not-so-hidden secret diagram of the Unknown Audio Device underground complex—also prominently displayed on the itch page—is almost certainly AI-generated.

The music is fine but feels like an afterthought: mainly breaky, acidfunk IDM that could have been made any time this century. “COPENHAGEN” is head-nodding techsteppy drum n’ bass. “MINIMALIZM” is a downtempo number that makes emotive use of what may be a ney reed flute (or more likely a convincing VST replica). On the other hand, “OMNILUNA” contains baroque piano chords that seem incongruous for the project as a whole, and several tracks including “DARKSHADOW” break off abruptly instead of tapering out. Ironically, the most appropriate use of Unknown Audio Device is not as an art-object but as ‘flow’-like decor cast by projector on a chill-out room wall or at a LAN party. But there are worse fates than effective vibe curation. (Marcello Ursic)
The Daily Heller: The Newly Inflated Career of Tony Sarg
Long forgotten by many, Sarg’s art and career get a gust of new life in an exhibition at the Norman Rockwell Museum.

One of my favorite childhood memories is watching the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day parade at balloon-eye-level from my cousin’s elegant Art Deco Century apartment building in New York City. One of my favorite books during those same youthful years was Tony Sarg’s New York , a collection of full-page illustrations looking down on well-known New York City attractions, including one at the intersection of 23rd Street and Fifth Avenue and Broadway. Little did I know in my youth that these two favorites would come together in artistic unity.

Sarg, a whimsical illustrator, puppeteer and designer—a very visible fixture on the New York popular art scene—was among the initial designers of original Thanksgiving Day Parade floats and balloons. He was also a prolific mapmaker for events like the 1939 New York World’s Fair and other distinctly NYC spectaculars. Long forgotten by many, his art and career got a renewed burst of interest during a 2023 exhibition, thanks to chief curator Stephanie Haboush Plunkett and guest curator Lenore D. Miller.

“Exploring themes relating to Sarg’s prolific career and ongoing influence, this theatrical installation serves as a window into the creative process and achievements of an exceptional American artist and showman,” says Plunkett. Exhibition themes include: London to New York: Sarg as Illustrator; Moving Images: Sarg’s Animations; Balloons Over Broadway: Macy’s on Parade; Puppets on Tour: Sarg’s Marionettes; Humor, Fantasy and the Turning Page; The Big Stage: Illustrated Maps, Architectural Projects and Two World’s Fairs; Whimsical Art for Commerce; Sarg’s Nantucket Adventures; and The Artist’s Legacy. An exhibition video and audio tour featuring noted commentators enhance the visitor experience, and a richly illustrated catalog (Abbeville Press) accompanies the show.

Born in Guatemala in 1880 to a diplomatic family, his life was peripatetic. While living in New York, Sarg immersed himself in the worlds of art and publishing and received illustration commissions from The Saturday Evening Post , Boy’s Life , American Girl , Ladies’ Home Journal , Good Housekeeping and Vanity Fair , among others, but he distinguished himself from other artists through puppetry, giving his first performance in his studio in the famed Flatiron Building. In 1917, he began performances of Franz von Pocci’s The Three Wishes , and in 1919, The Rose and the Ring opened on Broadway. In 1921, Rip Van Winkle became the first of his large touring shows, followed by Don Quixote , Treasure Island , The Chinese Willow Plate and Ali Baba . His production of Alice in Wonderland was especially popular, playing to millions at the Century of Progress World’s Fair in Chicago in 1933. Sinbad the Sailor , Robinson Crusoe and The Mikado were among his other productions, with Robin Hood (1939) as the last, due to the company’s financial challenges.

Sarg also designed murals and products for prominent New York hotels and department stores and opened popular toy shops in New York City. Of his body of work, puppeteer and historian Paul McPharlin noted that it “set up an ideal of American puppetry: a good play, as a rule, based on a familiar tale, with production details carefully worked out and integrated. Puppetry, scenery, lights, properties, and even the printed program, exhibited artistry. His bent for gaiety and humor, his love of odd effects, animals and the marvelous, found just the right combination.”
‘Pay attention and stay curious’: Réka Matyas on her charming little worlds filled with spotty dogs and…
The Budapest-based illustrator fills her colourful drawings with curious characters and unexpected details, encouraging us to slow down and find joy in the everyday. Spend a few minutes in…
The Budapest-based illustrator fills her colourful drawings with curious characters and unexpected details, encouraging us to slow down and find joy in the everyday.

Spend a few minutes in Réka Mátyás ’ portfolio, and you’ll meet two spotty dogs gazing at each other across a green meadow, a polka-dot cat posing beside an equally polka-dot tabi shoe, and a woman with ladybugs crawling through her golden hair. Polka-dot sisters, three cats stretched out across a chocolate-brown page, and a figure cradling a birthday cake with a single lit candle appear. It all feels soft, warm and slightly odd, splashed in a playful palette of bubblegum pinks, grassy greens and buttery yellows.

The Budapest-based illustrator and motion designer was born in Transylvania, Romania, and began her creative journey at university, where she studied Fine Arts and graduated with a BA in 2022. She experimented with all sorts of materials and mediums, though pencil sketches and realistic drawing were her real loves. By the end of her degree, she admits, she “felt quite lost”, with plenty of pressure to find her own style. So she took a year off and landed a role at a small creative studio as a motion designer, where she picked up the software, dabbled in graphic design, and started to see new possibilities. That led her to Budapest for a master’s in Graphic Design, which she completed in 2025. Today, she works full-time as a motion designer at Artbinary, “an amazing agency where I feel like part of the family”, while illustration fills her free time, along with the occasional graphic design project when something resonates.

For a long while, Réka felt she had to pick one path out of the three. “It stressed me out quite a bit,” she says. “But over time, I’ve learned to embrace all three, and I finally feel like I’ve found my place. I’ve also realised that switching between them keeps me creatively fresh. Each discipline gives me a different perspective and a little breathing room from the others, allowing me to return to my work with new ideas and push it in directions I might not have discovered otherwise. Now, rather than seeing these different paths as competing with each other, I see them as things that feed into and strengthen one another.”

With the world around her as her muse, Réka’s ideas usually come from everyday moments. “I’m interested in observing people, their lives and the little moments that might seem insignificant at first,” she says. Réka then jots these observations down or makes quick sketches in a notebook, where an idea might sit for months before it finds its way into an illustration. Nature, music, films and whatever book she’s reading chip in too, because “you just have to pay attention and stay curious”.

When the time comes to make something, Réka sits quietly for a few minutes and lets her mind wander, imagining a little scenario around the theme. Then comes lots of tiny, rough pencil or coloured-pen sketches. “They’re usually pretty ugly, and I almost always hate all of them at first!” she laughs, but this messy stage is where the final concept tends to appear, often somewhere completely different from where she started. Once something feels right, she plays with the composition, mood and colour, then moves to her iPad, which she says is usually the quickest part.

Among her favourites is an illustration for ZEITmagazine, commissioned by art director Viola Hasse, and her first editorial job. She had never drawn older people before, so she dived straight into sketching, starting with the couple at the centre – looking lovingly into each other’s eyes – and building a story around them with symbols and perspectives. Look closely, and you’ll spot a bird with a broken wing, which denotes the woman’s gradual loss of independence; pills; a pair of glasses; a water droplet and a character looking longingly in the distance. “I wanted the storytelling to feel subtle, rather than too literal, with little details that you could discover as you looked at the image,” she says. “I really enjoyed finding ways to translate the different layers of the story into small visual elements.”
Pattern Coffee is what happens when a Belfast branding studio becomes its own client
Fluent Format’s David Lewis on Pattern Coffee, the Belfast speciality coffee brand he’s built with Andile Cebekhulu as a side project, and what it taught them about clients. I’m a big fan…
Fluent Format’s David Lewis on Pattern Coffee, the Belfast speciality coffee brand he’s built with Andile Cebekhulu as a side project, and what it taught them about clients.

I’m a big fan of side projects. Creative Boom began as one, and look at it now. It seems I’m not alone. Every studio has one. The passionate thing on the side that gets talked about on a Friday afternoon, sketched out on paper, and then quietly forgotten about when Monday’s deadlines come in.

David Lewis and Andile Cebekhulu actually made theirs come true. David is the founder and creative director of Belfast brand and digital consultancy Fluent Format; Andile is its lead developer. By day, the pair build brands and digital experiences for other people. Alongside all that, they’ve been finding the time to build Pattern Coffee, a speciality coffee brand of their own.

Much like my platform, it began with no plan to be a business at all. The two friends spent nine months sourcing and trying coffees from around the world before deciding there was an opportunity. “We’re both dads with young families, busy jobs and a real love of coffee,” says David. “We joke that coffee is what keeps us going, but it’s also something we genuinely enjoy.”

What’s with the name, though? It came about during a phone call after work, when the pair got talking about how coffee had become part of their daily ritual – a moment to step away, reset and go again. Cue Pattern, along with a brand philosophy, ‘Your daily sweet spot’.
Graphic designers spend their working lives telling clients that brand matters. So can you imagine the pressure when it’s your own name on the packaging, and your own money behind it?

“We’ve always believed that a great brand can make a real difference to a business,” says David. “It’s not just about having a nice logo or packaging. It’s about creating something people recognise, connect with and want to be part of. Pattern gave us the chance to connect with and want to be part of. It gave us the chance to explore that from the very beginning, with complete creative freedom.”

I’m familiar with that freedom. It lets you go crazy without constraints. For David and Andile, it showed up most in the packaging. Because rather than go for the usual coffee tin, they developed a sleeve that follows the same silhouette of the bag, so the overall shape stays the same while each batch of coffee gets its own visual identity.
“We knew how the bag looked on a shop shelf was just as important as how it looked on someone’s kitchen counter,” explains David. “We wanted to create something people would enjoy having around.”
Wings, rugby and a snowball effect

Amazingly, there’s been no traditional marketing. Instead, Pattern has grown through small brand activations, like collaborations with running clubs and gyms, and even pop-ups at chicken wing shops – not, I admit, where I expected a speciality coffee brand to show up. But there you go.
The pair has also sponsored grassroots rugby, including women’s sports events, schools and universities, and supported Cancer Fund for Children on several occasions.

“We’ve found that the smallest things often have the biggest impact,” says David. “One collaboration leads to another, someone discovers the coffee and shares it with a friend, and before you know it, there’s a real snowball effect. It’s allowed us to build the brand and community we always wanted, without forcing it.”

But speciality coffee can feel intimidating when you think of all the tasting notes and brew ratios. Pattern is having none of that. “We love good coffee, but we don’t think you should have to know everything about it to enjoy it,” David continues. “We wanted Pattern to feel approachable, welcoming and something everyone could be part of.”

So what are the lessons from running a coffee brand on the side when you build brands for a living? Quite a lot. “It’s been a proper hustle getting it off the ground,” says David. “When you’re the one sourcing products, packing orders and investing your own money, you develop a completely different appreciation for the start-up founders you work with.”

Why Victorious Festival stopped selling its headliners and started selling Portsmouth
Portsmouth’s August bank holiday festival had a bit of a problem. Too many people were buying a ticket for one act on one day, then disappearing. Wildish & Co.’s solution is an identity…

Portsmouth’s August bank holiday festival had a bit of a problem. Too many people were buying a ticket for one act on one day, then disappearing. Wildish & Co.’s solution is an identity that puts the city first.

Who doesn’t love a good festival? I’ve been to my fair share over the last thirty years, and I can always tell you which bands were playing. The Prodigy in 1995 and Bowie in 2000, both at Glastonbury. Cypress Hill at V Festival in 2022 along with Asian Dub Foundation, I think it was. Björk at Bluedot a few years ago. Fun times.

If you’re running an event like this, you’ll know a lot hangs on your line-up. If it isn’t good enough, people simply won’t book. Victorious Festival knows this only too well. For more than a decade, the three-day event on Southsea seafront has drawn crowds from across the south of England, including Kings of Leon, Jamiroquai and Kasabian. But many of those only bought a ticket for a particular day, saw their fave act and went home. As such, each day felt like a different crowd, and that transience can be hard to build a community around.

A second line, ‘Portsmouth Says Welcome’, ties the brand to the city that hosts it. Perfect.

If you shift the story from who’s on stage to where you actually are and who you’re with, then a day ticket starts to look like you’re missing out.

The history behind the festival is also lovely. Victorious grew out of Portsmouth’s own music scene – its founders previously ran local venue Little Johnny Russell’s – and the new strategy includes a celebration of those humble roots.

Going back to the warm welcome, who’s it for? The identity launches alongside the 2027 line-up with large-scale posters at London Waterloo, Clapham Junction and Brighton, which shows you the target market.

Looking at the logo, it swaps the O in Victorious for a starburst borrowed from the sun on Portsmouth’s own coat of arms. Will you look at that – the city is quite literally in the middle of the name. The starburst also acts as an icon and is used across social, merchandise, wristbands and wayfinding.

There’s a custom headline typeface called Victorious Bold, which has tall, narrow capitals which stand out beautifully on everything from posters to stage screens. And the palette is taken right off the seafront – Navy, Sky, Sunset and Sunrise colours are complemented by secondary hues such as Sun Burn, Sea Spray and Sea Weed. A wave device runs through the lot, framing tickets, flags and signage. This was clearly a fun brief.

Then there are the illustrations, drawn in an engraving style and celebrating people enjoying themselves: a crab in headphones, for example, plus a sandcastle built from speakers and a seagull in a bucket hat. Remember those? Bucket hats were very handy when you needed to roll something out of the wind. Ahem.

A really nice touch is that every artist’s press photo gets a custom risograph-inspired treatment, so every act looks like part of the same thing. In other words, the headliners have been made to fit into Victorious’s world, when it has previously been the other way round.

Is the client happy? “Wildish & Co. got Victorious straight away,” says Leah Hennessy-Williams, head of PR and marketing at the festival. “They understood that what makes this festival special isn’t just who’s on stage, it’s the sea air, the city and the people who come back every single year. Adobe’s Eric Snowden on How AI Is Changing the Way Designers Work
AI was everywhere at Adobe MAX. In a conversation with Adobe’s Eric Snowden, I wanted to get specific about where it could actually help designers and what they’d want to keep doing…

Following the dialogue around Adobe MAX online felt very different from being there in person. We saw in real time what the programs could do—and reactions were definitely mixed. On Instagram and Threads, users were ready to cut ties with Adobe due to AI finding it’s way into every program in the creative suite. At MAX, though, it seemed to me that the purpose behind creating entry points for AI was all about creating efficiency for the user. Creativity was and will always be at the forefront of Adobe’s products, so how can they create a narrative that designers will feel better about when it comes to the programs they have used and loved for so many years?

I put that question to Eric Snowden, Adobe’s Senior Vice President of Design. I’d been reading research led by the University of Exeter’s Saeema Ahmed-Kristensen into how people and ChatGPT generate ideas for design tasks. Ahmed-Kristensen found that the model could produce ideas in volume, but its suggestions tended to cluster around similar concepts. I was curious about how Adobe could help designers see where AI was expanding their options and where their own judgment was shaping the work.

Snowden went back to a notable demo previewed at MAX, the grid demo. The designer asks the agent to lay out images or check brand colors while they work on something else in the same document. “You can use AI without ever generating anything,” Snowden said. It makes us think that the purpose of AI is to assist rather than to create.

I thought about how often I’ve gone through a file at the end of a project looking for the one thing I might have missed. Is every artboard using the approved palette? Are the images ready to go to press? Snowden pointed to an InDesign example that checked whether images were print-ready. I could see that being a major plus on a deadline, when the person who designed the piece is also the last person to review it before it goes out.

Adobe’s Disney example was at the other end of the spectrum. Snowden described how Disney uses its archive to build a custom model and iterate within an established visual world. When I asked what that looked like for an independent studio that is not at the magnitude of Disney, or an independent designer, he described a much smaller starting point. A team could bring in a logo, a typeface, and a few colors, then ask the software to flag where a document strays from the palette.

Later in our conversation, Snowden described using an agent in After Effects to rough out an animation. He went into the keyframes and adjusted the movement himself. When he decided the piece should run for 10 seconds instead of 20, he asked the agent to retime it, then went back in to tweak what he didn’t like.

That example gave me a better sense of what Adobe’s approach could mean in practice. Snowden could make a call about the pacing, delegate the work of shifting dozens of layers, and still get into the file to change how a particular moment landed. An editor might being more willing to try out a shorter or riskier cut if finding out whether it works only takes a few minutes in the background. I can also imagine wanting to explore a series of adjustments to the exact moment a title comes in, because a few frames can change how the whole sequence feels.

Productivity came up often at MAX, but Snowden seemed most excited to share what designers could do with the time they get back. A team could use it to try a direction it would ordinarily drop because the deadline is too close. An independent designer could work through another animation pass or show a client an idea that would otherwise stay in the sketchbook. Of course, that time could just as easily go toward producing more versions on a tighter schedule. The software can make either outcome possible.

I left MAX thinking about the distinction Snowden made near the end of our conversation. “It’s now easier than ever to make something above average,” he said. “I don’t think it’s any easier to make something great, frankly.” Which leads us to what we’ve all seen in the AI wild: logos, posters, and menus are executed every day that often seem somewhere above average, but rarely…

Run with the Semi-Wild Yilki Horses of Anatolia in Nur Tucker’s Captivating Photos
In 'The Untold Story of the Yilki Horse,' the British-Turkish photographer captures a portrait of the region's living heritage.

Around the dusty plains and otherworldly volcanic rock formations of the historical region of Cappadocia , a millennia-old tradition continues. Here in Central Anatolia, Turkey, horses have been a part of daily life, civic programs, and military campaigns since prehistory. In The Untold Story of the Yilki Horse , photographer Nur Tucker captures a portrait of the region’s living heritage.

Published by Hemeria, the title delves into the beauty and tenacity of the semi-wild horses while also highlighting the lifestyles of those who herd them through rugged landscapes. Tucker, who is a British-Turkish photographer based in the U.K., has long been drawn to the vigor and elegance of horses, and the yilki breed that populates Anatolia have a particularly resonant history.

“Yilki” comes from the Turkish verb yılmak , which means “to flee” or “to be set loose.” The name “has come to describe the condition of these herds that live between liberation and loss, between domestic heritage and wild abandon,” says a statement.

In a place where horses have been bred for agriculture, transportation, battle, and more for thousands of years, their role forever changed within just the past century due to mechanization and industrialization. With motorized tractors, trucks, and cars to work the fields and provide transportation, horses essentially became redundant. Released to fend for themselves, they survived harsh winters, bred on their own, and grew into sizable herds. In The Untold Story of the Yilki Horse, Tucker composes a love letter to these striking animals, celebrating their resilience through more than 100 images.
The book is now available for purchase directly from Hemeria , and it’s slated for worldwide release next October. See more on Tucker’s Instagram .

Helen Bur’s Monumental Bordeaux Mural Celebrates Motherhood and Female Solidarity, France
British street artist Helen Bur completes her largest mural to date in Bordeaux's Grand Parc neighbourhood, celebrating motherhood, female solidarity and community connection through EXIT's…

British street artist Helen Bur has completed her largest mural to date in Bordeaux, France, transforming the towering façade of the Nerval residential building in the Grand Parc neighbourhood into a monumental portrait of motherhood, female solidarity and human connection. Entitled Matrescense , the artwork depicts two local women in the final trimester of pregnancy, brought together through a project that celebrates the importance of companionship and mutual support within the community.
Helen Bur, WIP, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

The title, Matrescence , refers to the profound transition into motherhood, a developmental process encompassing the physical, psychological, emotional and social changes experienced as a woman becomes a mother. Much like adolescence, it is a period of transformation in which identity, relationships and perceptions of self evolve.

Through her portrayal of two expectant mothers, Helen Bur gives this often overlooked experience a monumental public presence, recognising not only the vulnerability and anticipation of pregnancy but also the importance of connection, understanding and mutual support during one of life’s most significant transitions.
Matrescense, Helen Bur, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

Created for KIFKIF, an ambitious urban art initiative led by Bordeaux-based association EXIT, the mural marks the beginning of a wider programme connecting internationally recognised artists with local residents through public art, creative workshops and community participation.

At the heart of Matrescense are two pregnant women arranged head-to-foot, their bodies forming an intimate, almost circular composition reminiscent of the yin-yang symbol. One reclines towards the ground while the other turns upwards, their opposing positions creating a sense of balance and interdependence. Although each woman occupies her own space within the painting, their gestures and proximity suggest an unspoken relationship built upon understanding, companionship and mutual care.
In detail: Matrescense, Helen Bur, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

Both women live in Bordeaux’s Grand Parc neighbourhood and were invited to become models for the artwork. Remarkably, they had not known one another before the project, making their connection something that developed through the creative process itself. What appears to be a longstanding bond between two women was, in fact, formed through the experience of participating in the mural.
In detail: Matrescense, Helen Bur, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

The subject emerged from Helen Bur’s exploration of the neighbourhood’s social realities, particularly the experiences of women raising children without a partner. Rather than portraying motherhood through an idealised image of the family, she places two expectant mothers together, acknowledging the friendships, relationships and wider networks of support that can become essential throughout pregnancy and parenthood.
Matrescense: Intimacy on a Monumental Scale

Rising across the façade of the Nerval building, the 32-metre mural transforms an ordinary residential elevation into an expansive, deeply personal painting. Completed following more than two weeks on site, despite challenging weather conditions, the work represents a significant milestone in Bur’s artistic practice.
In detail: Matrescense, Helen Bur, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

The composition is particularly striking for the contrast between its monumental scale and the intimacy of its subject. The two women appear suspended within a richly layered interior of deep terracotta, warm ochre and patterned textiles, surrounded by abundant green foliage. The arrangement creates the impression of a private domestic space opened to the city, allowing an everyday moment of connection to occupy the architecture of an entire building.
In detail: Matrescense, Helen Bur, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

A federal judge has extended her block on construction of President Trump's D.C. arch for two weeks, another short-term victory for those who don't want to see the 250-foot structure break ground.

D.C. District Judge Tanya Chutkan extended her temporary restraining order on Wednesday, the day before it was set to expire. She originally stepped in to block construction on the night of Nov. 5, after the National Capital Planning Commission and National Park Service gave the arch final approval and the Trump administration said construction could begin imminently.
Democrats want to stop Trump's arch, golf course and more. What are their options?

Chutkan's new five-page order prevents the administration from "initiating, making, or otherwise effectuating any construction, excavation, demolition, land-disturbance, utility-installation, or roadway-closure activity, or any other construction-related activity" at Memorial Circle through Dec. 3.

"The judge's order recognizes that the conditions that called for emergency relief two weeks ago remain unchanged," Nick Sansone, the Public Citizen attorney representing the original plaintiffs in the lawsuit, said in a statement .
The extension gives Chutkan more time to consider plaintiffs' request for a longer-term preliminary injunction, which would prohibit construction as the lawsuit against the arch plays out.
That lawsuit started earlier this year with a challenge from a group of Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian, but has expanded in recent weeks.

In late October, the governments of D.C. and Virginia filed another lawsuit, which was combined with the original. And nine members of the Kennedy family joined the fight last week, saying the arch will block historic sightlines and cast shadows over the graves of John F. Kennedy and others at nearby Arlington National Cemetery.
Kennedy relatives join the fight against Trump's arch, alleging harm to JFK's grave

"This is one man who wants to build this arch. He's violated every rule. If this is a great idea, then bring it before Congress, follow the rules and get it approved," Max Kennedy, a son of Robert F. Kennedy, told NPR's All Things Considered .
Opposition to the arch — from area residents, veterans, local officials, Democratic lawmakers and more — has grown in recent months as the structure hurtled through the federal approval process.

Critics take issue with the arch's scale and location , saying it would interrupt the solemn and historic vista between Arlington National Cemetery and the Lincoln Memorial. Plaintiffs argue the structure violates several laws — including the Commemorative Works Act and D.C.'s Height of Buildings Act — and is fundamentally illegal without approval from Congress.
A jogger passes a mobile security camera truck at Memorial Circle, where Trump wants to build his arch.
The Trump administration has not sought that approval, arguing the arch is covered by Congress' authorization in 1925 of a pair of 166-foot columns at the same location, which were never built.

In court filings and a recently unveiled website , the administration characterizes building the arch as a matter of urgency — both to complete that century-old vision and to facilitate national security . Trump said in September that the arch would double as a military complex, but the plans that got final approval this month don't include any details to that effect.

In a declaration this week , Ricky Buria, chief of staff to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, told the court that the agency is "currently in the planning process to determine how to integrate national defense uses … into the Arch without changing the existing plans for the Arch."

OUTSIDE IN: New Exhibition at GraffitiStreet Gallery, Chichester
What happens when art made for walls, rooftops and railway lines comes indoors? OUTSIDE IN brings internationally recognised street artists to GraffitiStreet Gallery, Chichester, exploring…

What happens when art made for walls, rooftops and railway lines comes indoors? This November 20th, GraffitiStreet Gallery presents OUTSIDE IN, a group exhibition bringing together internationally recognised artists whose practices are rooted in graffiti and street art. Exploring the journey from public space to the studio, the exhibition considers how an artist’s distinctive visual language moves between different settings, scales and materials, and how these transitions change the way we experience their work.

A graffiti tag, a mural spanning a building, a canvas contained within a frame and a sculpture within the gallery each create a different encounter with the viewer. Site can amplify or redirect meaning, scale can alter our response, and material can reveal another dimension of an artist’s practice. Yet across these shifts, the symbols, ideas and signature styles that define each artist remain unmistakable. How much of urban art is bound to its setting, and how much travels with the artist?
As the street enters the gallery, OUTSIDE IN invites visitors to discover what changes, what intensifies and what endures.

German artist Case Maclaim , a pioneer of photorealist graffiti, moves between monumental murals and intimate studio paintings, bringing the technical precision and extraordinary attention to detail that have defined his practice into a more concentrated setting.

Spanish duo PichiAvo unite classical sculpture and graffiti, bringing ancient mythology into dialogue with contemporary urban culture. Their distinctive compositions challenge the boundaries between artistic traditions, allowing the language of the street to coexist with the enduring influence of classical art.

South African artist Faith47 , internationally recognised for her poetic large-scale murals, extends her practice into sculpture, exploring how familiar themes and imagery acquire a different physical presence through material and form.

British artist My Dog Sighs transforms overlooked objects and unconventional surfaces into emotionally resonant artworks, while Sweet Toof brings the irreverence of his unmistakable teeth motif into paintings that connect graffiti, portraiture and art history.

Belgian artist Joachim Lambrechts balances spontaneous mark-making with carefully considered compositions, while South African artist Sonny Sundancer explores the expressive possibilities of abstraction beyond his large-scale street practice. Nean Kingdom , whose distinctive imagery has become an instantly recognisable part of his artistic identity, similarly demonstrates how a visual language developed through street art can retain its character in the studio.

Although their approaches differ considerably, each artist offers a perspective on the relationship between artistic identity and environment. Moving between the street and the studio becomes more than a change of location; it creates opportunities to experiment with materials, reconsider scale and develop ideas beyond the conditions in which their practices first emerged.
An Exhibition Across Materials and Disciplines

Alongside the featured artists, OUTSIDE [IN] includes selected artworks and collectables by Banksy, STIK and TOX, bringing further dimensions to the exhibition’s exploration of graffiti and street art.

From the repetition of a graffiti tag to the intimacy of a painting, the exhibition reveals how urban art continues to evolve across disciplines while retaining its connection to the visual culture of the street.

Together, these diverse practices create an opportunity to experience familiar artistic languages in an entirely different context, encouraging visitors to look beyond the surface and consider the ideas, techniques and identities that give each artist’s work its distinctive character.

JM Brea Paints the Moment Before the Crucifixion in Montehermoso
JM Brea has painted La Crucifixión del Cristo de los Remedios outside the chapel of the Santísimo Cristo de los Remedios in Montehermoso, Spain. Made for the town council, the mural stops…

JM Brea has painted La Crucifixión del Cristo de los Remedios outside the chapel of the Santísimo Cristo de los Remedios in Montehermoso, Spain. Made for the town council, the mural stops just before the first nail is driven through Christ’s hand. Brea places the moment of impending violence beside a chapel whose altar holds an image of the crucified Christ.

In Brea’s account of the composition, Christ’s hand rests against the wood of the cross while a nail is held over its palm. The action has not yet happened: the pointed nail and the waiting hand carry the tension. Brea describes the treatment as Baroque in character, a choice tied to the chapel rather than simply to the biblical subject.

The painting also draws on details at the site. Three nails represented at the top of the main altarpiece find an echo in the mural’s single poised nail and the shadow of three fingers across the painted wood, according to Brea. Outside, three granite crosses stand near the chapel. These connections give the work a particular setting: its scene begins on the exterior wall, while the crucifixion appears in the sculpture inside.

Montehermoso’s town council dates the chapel to the 16th century and describes it as regional Baroque in style. The image of the Cristo de los Remedios inside is from the 18th century. The chapel remains associated with the Feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross and devotions to Christ of the Remedies, making Brea’s subject closely bound to the building’s use as well as its decoration.

The mural is part of Vientos del Pueblo, a literary and cultural route developed with Montehermoso’s schools and local partners. The project links artistic work in the town to education and local heritage. Brea’s contribution is grounded in one place: the chapel, its crosses and the image encountered within.

The leap from RKO Radio Pictures circa 1940 to Paul Schrader in the 1980s is like chasing store-brand vanilla ice cream with Cold Stone’s Cat in the Hat’s Cotton Candy Catastrophe. That’s not to label old-school Hollywood as drab and droll, but rather to emphasize Schrader’s hold-on-to-your-butts creativity. Jacques Tourneur ’s Cat People (1942) is a black-and-white romantic thriller that coyly teases a domestic nightmare about animalian transformations, but it’s prim and proper for the times .
That’s the glory of early cinema: filmic simplicity, where storytelling has nowhere to hide.

Generational time-jumps like The Blob or The Fly have become seminal examples of horror remakes that justify their way-later revamps; Cat People (1982) deserves similar praise. It’s a shame that David Bowie ’s “ Cat People (Putting Out Fire) ” theme song might be more popular than the film outside genre circles, although fair game, because that was me at one point.

Universal Pictures wasn’t afraid to greenlight a sexually explicit werecat flick for the masses, albeit a harder sell than Poltergeist , Halloween III: Season of the Witch , and other genre titles released the same year.
The 1980s were strange times, and it doesn’t get much stranger than Cat People.

DeWitt Bodeen ’s New Yorker fantasy script bathes in the gender-role stickiness of 1940s cinema, as a magnificent time capsule of martini lunches and wedding bell normalcy. Writer Alan Ormsby ’s many-years-later update couldn’t be further removed, taking the free-spirited erotic route to creature-feature ferocity. Both films are about forbidden lust and sexual consequences, and yet Schrader oversees a far zanier and bolder version. Tourneur thickens tension with questions about whether there’s supernatural mystery afoot. In contrast, Schrader’s first sequence reveals an offworld realm where people are tethered to feline excellence—one grounded, the other gonzo.

German actress Nastassja Kinski stars as Irena Gallier, once orphaned and now a beautiful virgin visiting her brother Paul ( Malcolm McDowell ) in New Orleans for the first time. She learns, ever so awkwardly, that her and Pual’s lineage ties to a community of black leopard worshippers who pass souls through big-cat bodies, and that’s hardly Irena’s wildest discovery. After Irena strikes a hot-and-heavy relationship with New Orleans zoo curator Oliver Yates ( John Heard ), Paul confesses that any intimate extracurriculars will turn Irena into her murderous animal equivalent. The only safe option would be to inbreed, but Irena won’t comply. Thus kickstarts Irena’s adventure through New Orleans: a confused shapeshifter who doesn’t want to kill, yet craves all the same carnal pleasures of regular humans.

Schrader sheds the Pleasantville-era blueprints of 1942’s Cat People for a freakier, fetishistic take on primality. Bodeen pokes and prods Simone Simon ’s Irena Dubrovna from a male-dominated perspective, yet holds back the jungle inspirations of jet-black jaguars kept behind iron bars for a last-second reveal. Ormsby’s horror-centric collaborations with Bob Clark and Joe Dante make sense, given how his Cat People invokes werewolf comparisons, dispelling any concerns that surreality will be held for the third act. Paul wastes no time assuring audiences that 1982’s Cat People wants to platform its Species -like mindset—pre- Species , of course.

It’s not only a magnificent film, but a magnificent remake as well. Kinski’s Irena is freed from her original villain label, embracing the more liberated ideologies of the 1980s, which led to McDowell’s fantastic casting as an antagonistic Paul. There’s no desire to reuse Bodeen’s outdated societal dynamics or Tourneur’s traditional cinematic style. Schrader leans into the gothic haunts of New Orleans while famously aiming for “ more skin than blood, ” turning it into a sweaty, panting address of sinful pleasures.

Only two sequences remain from the original: Annette O’Toole ’s jogging sequence as Alice, where she’s stalked like Jane Randolph ’s assistant, and the swimming pool sequence, where Irena’s cat-like growls taunt Alice. Schrader is far more interested in these Dune…
