Why Oliver Reed Was One of Horror’s Greatest Scream Kings
The arrival of Ken Russell’s uncut version of The Devils (1971) in theaters this year has not only kindled interest in the films of the director but also in the work of the film’s star…

The arrival of Ken Russell ’s uncut version of The Devils (1971) in theaters this year has not only kindled interest in the films of the director but also in the work of the film’s star, Oliver Reed .

One of England’s legendary hell-raisers , Reed rose to fame at Hammer Studios , England’s House of Horrors, in the early 1960s. As his star rose, he continued to return to the horror genre, sometimes out of necessity perhaps, but also because of the lure of the material, making him one of the greatest Scream Kings of his generation.

Though not conventionally handsome in the Carey Grant, Paul Newman mold, Reed had an undeniable charisma and animal magnetism that positively erupted from the screen, making his film appearances, from brief cameos to leading roles, indelible and unforgettable.

Reed had landed a few bit roles in the late 1950s, but his career did not really get rolling until Hammer came calling at the end of the decade. In 1959, Reed was invited by one of Hammer’s casting directors, Stuart Lyons , to audition for the studio , and he was eventually cast in a small role in The Two Faces of Dr. Jekyll (1960). He appears in one scene as a bouncer and delivers a couple of lines before being subdued in a would-be barroom brawl by Christopher Lee and Paul Massie .

Still, his work on the film garnered the attention and praise of director Terrence Fisher , who around this time said, “Were I invited to predict sure stardom for an unknown young actor of today, and asked to back that prediction with a heavy bet, the youngster I’d pick would be 22-year-old Mr. Reed.”

Reed won his first leading role over seventeen other young hopefuls to play Leon in Curse of the Werewolf (1961). Though not a hit at the time, the film has become a classic of Hammer horror and the werewolf subgenre. Reed gives a performance of nuance and pathos , expressing the torment of his split nature. Where he truly excels, however, is in his performance as the werewolf, which gives him an opportunity to showcase his remarkable physical presence and abilities. In a way, it was something of an omen for his career and personal life to come . Many have joked that his first big role was as a werewolf and then he went on to become one in real life as his drinking and macho persona became more grandiose.

Another early role was in Captain Clegg , aka Night Creatures (1962), in which he plays the male half of the romantic subplot. The film is odd in that it is more of a swashbuckling semi-comedy than a horror film , and Reed’s performance is rather starchy and stiff. It seems that Hammer wasn’t quite sure how to use Reed yet, but it was still an opportunity to appear in a high-profile film for the studio alongside the legendary Peter Cushing . In one scene, Reed played up the pain of an injury. Observing this, Cushing told him (by some accounts in person, by others in a letter), “If somebody grabs you, just blink. The screen is so big that even the slightest movement makes the point.” Cushing’s “less is more” advice stuck with Reed throughout the rest of his career and informed practically every performance to come .

Two other offerings from Hammer presaged the kinds of roles that Reed would excel in throughout the coming years. The Damned (1962) was Hammer’s answer to Village of the Damned , featuring children with unique intellectual and telekinetic gifts. The most memorable aspect of the film is the first half, which features Reed as King, the leader of a group of violent delinquents. Many have noted that this section of the film presages the kinds of gang dynamics and stylized violence found in Stanley Kubrick’s A Clockwork Orange nearly a decade later.

In Paranoiac (1963), Reed plays Simon Ashby, the pampered son of nobility who has reached the bottom of his bank account . Reed gets to spend much of the movie in what feels like his element—drinking heavily and recklessly driving his roadster. It is an excellent performance and an exceptional Hammer film directed by legendary cinematographer Freddie Francis , fresh off his work on the haunted house classic The Innocents (1961).
The Treasure of La Buse: The $1 billion secret of The Seychelles

I know that the real history of pirates is one we probably shouldn’t romanticise as much as we do, but still, people like Olivier Levasseur, or La Buse if ya nasty, make it incredibly easy to do just that.

Levasseur was a native of Calais who earned notoriety in the early 1700s as a feared and respected pirate who operated in the Caribbean and Indian Ocean. While he was known for his ruthlessness and ferocity, that wasn’t what really made his name. His nickname came due to his very specific modus operandi. If you were sailing a merchant ship through quiet waters, he had this way of flitting his ship out of nowhere with truly uncanny speed. This meant people started referring to him as The Buzzard, or La Buse in his native tongue.

La Buse was a force to be reckoned with. Able to track prey for months, waiting for the moment they drop their guard to strike. This wasn’t just his method day to day, though; this was the method that secured him one of the biggest scores of the Golden Age of Piracy. In April 1721, La Buse partnered with English pirate John Taylor to take down a ship that couldn’t be more of a tantalising prospect for a pirate if it contained the heart of Davy Jones himself.

Anchored on Réunion Island off the coast of Madagascar was the Portuguese Galleon Our Lady of the Cape. This was a ship carrying the entire combined wealth of the Portuguese Viceroy to India and the Archbishop of Goa that had been caught in a storm so severe it needed to anchor for urgent repairs. That’s more, it only survived the storm because its crew threw its entire, 72-strong supply of cannons overboard. It was a sitting duck, so Levasseur and Taylor took it.

Taylor took his share of the loot and fled to the Americas while Levasseur remained on the seas, his reputation at an all-time high and public enemy number one for the Portuguese Navy. He evaded capture for the next nine years until he was finally captured in 1730. Fittingly enough, he was brought back to Réunion Island, the site of his greatest triumph, for his execution, when he caused an uproar while on the gallows for his hanging.

With the bag over his head and the noose around his neck, La Buse tore his necklace off, revealed that it contained a parchment and just before his death, shouted to the assembled crowd, “Find my treasure, we who may understand it!”

He dropped, but no one was watching. People were too busy fighting over what they thought was a map leading to incalculable amounts of treasure. The person who found it, however, may have felt a little shortchanged, as it wasn’t a map.

It was a cypher. A set of deeply cryptic riddles that people have spent the centuries since trying and failing to uncover, with legend saying that La Buse’s treasure still lies somewhere on either Réunion Island or the nearby Seychelles, two island paradises that might just have a treasure haul valued at well over a billion dollars buried somewhere on their coasts. Except this is a pirate story. I mention that they’re easy to romanticise because the vast majority of them are exactly that. Romances in the classic sense of the word where everything is enhanced for poetry and drama.

We have the records of Levasseur’s execution, and they make no mention of his cypher. It only surfaced in the 1930s when a French historian claimed to have discovered and published it, so its truth is a very distant possibility. However, everything up until that point is a hundred per cent true, and we know this because in 2025, the wreck of Our Lady of the Cape was discovered near Madagascar. We have the records from the Portuguese government of the time confirming its cargo when La Buse and Taylor attacked.
None of it was found on the wreck. Perhaps the cypher isn’t real, but maybe the treasure itself could still be out there for the soul daring enough to find it?

Fans of developers FakeFish and Undertow Games’ Bartrauma will have new content to devour next week when the “Home & Harbor” Expansion arrives on December 2 . Before then, the devteams have released a Dev Diary for the expansion that takes players deeper into the story, look and technology of the mysterious Descendants.

The Descendants were one of Europa’s original factions, alongside the Jovian People’s Movement and the Europa Coalition. They vanished around the time contact with Earth was severed, leaving behind no bodies and no signs of violence. In the Home & Harbor Expansion they suddenly reappear, with the player caught in the middle of it.

The Dev Diary also reveals the thinking behind the faction’s NASA-punk art direction, the Singularity Reactor, a new high-risk, high-reward reactor that can power the Descendants’ far more power-hungry devices, and the cybernetic technology they use to enhance both themselves and their servant creatures.

The Home & Harbor Expansion adds player-owned Outposts to the acclaimed sci-fi submarine simulator, letting players own, build, customize, manage and defend their own homes. It also introduces the mysterious technocratic Descendants, a new faction bringing fresh story, gameplay, lore, weapons and submarines.

Originally launching into Early Access back in 2019 for PC via Steam , Barotrauma is a sci-fi submarine simulator with survival horror elements. In the not too distant future, humanity has fled to Jupiter’s moon. Due to the hostile surface of the moon, life can only be found in the ocean below. You’ll take command of one of a submarine and its crew, upgrading it as you go while exploring the depths and dealing with the various monsters that lurk in the deep that will look to invade your sub.
Review: ‘Am I Nima’ Provides an Unnerving Yet Fascinating Story Experience
Many other forms of media create stories that have you sit with discomfort, but it’s harder to pull off in a video game. With the medium being so active, it needs the player to want to…

Many other forms of media create stories that have you sit with discomfort, but it’s harder to pull off in a video game. With the medium being so active, it needs the player to want to continue for the story to move forward. If it’s making the player squirm, they’ll often put the controller down rather than pushing onwards. But like the best examples of uncomfortable cinema, strong storytelling can keep you engaged, even when you have to continue pressing buttons.

Am I Nima , a psychological horror game from HO! Games, is one of the most uncomfortable games I’ve played in a while, and I mean that as a compliment. It’s a visual novel that explores extremely heavy themes using a unique mechanic that revolves around creating thoughts by combining words you learn through conversation and exploration.

You play Nima, a young girl who lost her memories in an accident. She’s being locked up in the basement by her mother, who runs her through a series of tests to prove that you are indeed Nima. These tests can be grueling physically, mentally, and morally, creating a deeply unsettling narrative that’s full of mystery and uncertainty. Between these conversations with your mother, you are also given a chance to explore your room, which provides the opportunity to learn a little more about your life before the accident.

Rather than just drive the narrative forwards with simple dialogue choices like most visual novels, Am I Nima uses a clever word-based mechanic to not only dictate what you can say, but also cleverly give interiority to the main character. On your screen, you have a brain space on the right side, with Nima’s head under it. As a reaction to certain bits of conversation, words will pop into your mind, demonstrating how she’s reacting to what she hears. For example, since she’s an amnesiac, the first time she hears her mother, the word “stranger” shows up in her head. When you’re prompted for a response, you can drag a word from your mind into your head, which will give you a response you can elect to say.

Combining words will yield new words, not only giving you new options, but also again revealing some part of how Nima’s mind interprets things. It’s an interesting experience, because sometimes it feels like a natural result that follows just from the definitions of the words, while other times it gives you an unexpected response that makes you stop in your tracks and try to understand exactly how she came to that conclusion. The way the game makes you responsible for figuring it out at times makes you such an active participant in the narrative, drawing you in just as much as the game’s writing.

Occasionally, the large amount of words you come across in the game does get a bit hard to manage, but there are a few tools to help you organize. All the words you’ve discovered are in a big list on the left side, and clicking on them will add them to your brain so you can start playing around with them. If your brain gets too full for you, you can always delete words to help it be easier to read. The list on the left can be sorted and searched, and if it helps you can mark certain words as favorites for easy access. You can even select an option that will highlight words that can be used as responses or will move the story forward if used.

In addition to conversations, which are always compelling, you’ll have times where you’re given free reign of a room to click around and examine things to add words to your library. This part makes it feel a bit more like an adventure game than a visual novel, experimenting with objects to see what it gets you. There’s even some light puzzle solving as the game progresses that helps add variety, even if these are quite as compelling as the rest of the game. By the end I felt the exploration was a bit more satisfying from a narrative standpoint than a mechanical one.

At the end of a day, you’re usually visited by dreams, which are lushly animated sequences that feature a small amount of voice work to make it stand out. These feel appropriately surreal, adding to the strange, nightmarish tone, but they aren’t just for style. Contained in the dreams are hints that will help you find specific words…

Callers diverted to sex line after public safety alert in Maryland due to storms
"No babe, I swear, I just wanted to know when the bridge was open!"

Maryland is one of several parts of America being battered by storms, high winds and non-stop rain, leading to a public safety alert being sent out on November 26th that claimed to contain the number to the Maryland Transportation Authority (MTA).

The Maryland Department of Emergency Management (MDTA) sent the alert at 3pm. It warned that the MTA had closed off the Bay Bridge as of 11.45 am that morning. This is a route that thousands of drivers a day use for their daily commute, yet the winds were so strong that even before the Authority closed the bridge entirely, they were preventing any tractor-box trailer combination with a combined weight of under 64,000 pounds from crossing due.

The message said to avoid the area and if that wasn’t possible, it provided a website and a phone number to contact for more information. Citizens who called the line were in for a monumental shock when they dialled the number and found themselves on the phone to a sex hotline.

MDTA spokesperson Brad Tanner said that the agency has since corrected the error, saying in a statement that “We recognize that it was an unfortunate error. We know it might have distressed Marylanders, but these alerts are critical to keeping people safe.”
The MDTA didn’t attempt to make light of the situation or see the funny side of it, as these storms were far more than just inclement weather.
Instead, they were the kind of heavy wind and rain that ripped the roof off an entire condominium in Ocean City and left over 100,000 citizens of the state without power.
The MDA announced the bridge was reopening later the same day, and the storms themselves are expected to ease up over the coming days, yet have caused chaos for many Americans’ Thanksgiving plans.

5 Hidden Gem Horror Movies from the Early 2000s Worth Revisiting

Horror fans may remember the early aughts as an era dominated by J-Horror and studio-backed remakes, but that has more to do with a generalized lack of independent marketing and distribution than a lack of quality horror flicks.

As a matter of fact, there were actually plenty of great genre movies that originally fell through the cracks but which are now easy to access thanks to the rise of streaming, VOD, and boutique physical media releases. That’s why I’ve decided to come up with this handy list recommending five criminally underrated horror films from the early 2000s that are worth revisiting.

As usual, this list is purely based on personal opinion, but I’ll be focusing on low-profile productions that were never given a proper chance to shine. That being said, don’t forget to comment below with your own favorites from the 2000s if you think I missed a particularly underrated movie.
With that out of the way, onto the list!

A single location slasher with a supernatural twist, Dave Payne’s Reeker is one of my favorite movies on this list, even if it’s not necessarily one of the best . The way I see it , this highly atmospheric thriller makes up for most of its narrative blunders and low production value with sheer creativity and a memorable villain that should have appeared in many more sequels.

This mind-bending horror yarn may not be for everyone, with the final plot twist dividing genre fans to this very day ( not even mentioning the trope-heavy dialogue) , but I still think that Reeker is a hell of a lot better than most critics gave it credit for back in 2005. If you like this one, I’d also recommend tracking down its surprisingly entertaining prequel , No Man’s Land: Rise of the Reeker .

Lucky McKee is one of the most underrated auteurs still active in the indie horror scene, so it makes sense that one of his films would show up on a list highlighting 2000s horror movies that deserve more love. While there are several McKee productions that could be included here, today I’d like to shine a light on his supernatural high school thriller The Woods .

A ’60s-set period piece about a troubled teenager who’s sent to live at an isolated private school with a dark history, The Woods dabbles in both good old-fashioned supernatural horror and post-modern humor that you could only get from a filmmaker aware that he’s playing with familiar gothic tropes.
Not only that, but you also get to see Bruce Campbell play our lead’s bumbling father, with his character alone already being worth the price of admission.

I’m pretty sure I’m not the only one who thinks that subways are inherently scary, but the London Underground takes the cake as one of the spookiest transit systems in the world . That’s why Christopher Smith’s urban slasher Creep is such a good time, with this underrated flick making the most of its claustrophobic setting.

Of course, it helps that Franka Potente makes for a charming protagonist that you can’t help but root for. The film’s cannibalistic killer is also surprisingly scary despite being a patchwork of well-known genre tropes, with the gruesome scares here being the main reason why I think Smith’s debut feature is worth revisiting over two decades later.
If you’re a fan of this one, don’t forget to check out Smith’s upcoming remake, now called The Creep , which is set to be released by Shudder.

Loosely based on a chilling true story, Zev Berman’s Borderland miraculously manages to balance both sensationalist schlock and serious horror as it exposes the dangers of uninformed tourism. While the experience starts out as more of a violent crime thriller than anything else, things eventually escalate into horror territory once we learn more about our deranged antagonists.

If the nightmarish “ Narcosatanists ” aren’t enough to convince you that Borderland is worth checking out, keep in mind that the flick also boasts some of the best practical gore effects of its era, as well as relatable characters with death scenes that often feel more tragic and unsettling than “ fun. ”

The South Korean band on how Moonrise Kingdom , anime, and more inspired their new record.

Mood Board is our column where artists share a few of the things that inspired their new record. This time, the members of the South Korean band LEENALCHI tell us how Moonrise Kingdom , anime, and more helped shape Sugungga — out now on Luaka Bop.
1. The school performance scene in the film Moonrise Kingdom
I found the scenes of numerous children wearing animal masks, moving between the stage and backstage, fantastical and beautiful.
2. Eric Timothy Carlson’s lyric video work
His lyric video work, featuring distinctive typography and symbolic graphics, was another point of reference.
3. “Mao Mao Mao” — the meaning behind the title

The “Mao” in the new song “Mao Mao Mao” comes from hajimao , a Korean expression meaning “don’t do it.” Because of the pronunciation, it also brings Mao Zedong and cats to mind. Those two associations stayed with me throughout the creative process.
4. Anime such as Nadia: The Secret of Blue Water and Future Boy Conan .

Rather than being inspired by anything in particular, I found myself thinking about anime I enjoyed as a child, such as Nadia: The Secret of Blue Water and Future Boy Conan . Perhaps it’s because they portray complex, weighty worlds in a playful way.
Florida man convicted of killing British woman he met on extreme fetish site
A Florida man has been convicted of murder by a U.S Jury for the killing of a British woman who allegedly expressed a desire to be murdered.

Florida prosecutors announced in a Facebook statement that Dwain Hall, 54, was found guilty of kidnapping and murdering Sonia Exelby, 32, and sentenced to two consecutive life terms, with the case called “extraordinary and deeply disturbing” by Bill Gladson, state attorney for the Fifth Judicial Circuit.

According to prosecutors, Hall and Exelby had known each other for two years before he murdered her. They had met on the now-defunct extreme fetish website “Motherless.com”, which court documents described as hosting “content that depicted various fetishes, including extreme BDSM, torture, and rape material.”
They had used the site, along with the encrypted application Sessions, to communicate ever since.
Hall, who went by the username “AlphaSadist” on the site, alleged that Exelby had expressed a desire to be murdered. On October 10th, 2025, she travelled to Gainesville, Florida to meet him.

Hall is accused of spending the next week sexually abusing her, before stabing her to death. CBS affiliate WPEC-TV reported that the arrest affidavit included an ominous message that Exelby, who had struggled with her mental health for a long time, sent to a friend of hers.

The message read, “ I’m sorry he keeps taking my phone he doesn’t trust me with it. He made it clear there was no way out unless I shoot him. I was questioning it last night. I can’t kill anyone. He’s in the shower, but I’m locked in, and there is no signal in the middle of nowhere.”

It continued, “I thought he’d do it quick and not give my mind time to stew and realise this is the last thing I’ll ever say to anyone if I don’t take his offer of shooting him. He showed me about to use it and where to aim it.”
Her body was found in a wooded area of Manon Oaks, Florida, near Hall’s home, seven days after she arrived in the country.

Exelby’s family made a statement to British Police last July that said, “Sonia was a truly beautiful person, inside and out. She was incredibly talented. Sonia could play the piano so effortlessly, and when she sang, she had the voice of an angel.”
Her family added, “Being around her felt special—she brought a calmness and warmth that made everything feel a little lighter.”

“Will We Grow or Decay?” — Rose Chamber Stare Down a Dying Society in Video for “Modern Rot”
You need no sympathy to understand what I say We’re a dying society.
You need no sympathy to understand what I say
We’re a dying society. Falling, being swept away

There are mornings when the present feels bleaker than any future you used to worry about. Before breakfast, you can read a dispatch from a bombed hospital, see someone ask strangers for help with rent, and have your stolen data trigger a targeted ad promising a full night’s sleep. You put the phone down because you’ve had enough and pick it up again because, like a Pavlovian dog, you are dying to know what the next tragedy is. That impulse gets a blunt diagnosis in Modern Rot, the opening track and first single from Rose Chamber ’s debut album, My Silhouette .

The track takes its time getting to the dance floor. A bell tolls through the opening synth tones as a drum hit echoes and a guitar squeals in the distance. A woman’s sampled voice comes through just before the darkwave beat and bass synth take over. The guitar holds a few low notes over the beat until they have the resonance of a piano with the sustain pedal down, reminiscent of “The Lord’s Prayer” by The Lords of the New Church. Vocalist Ace Stallings sings with Ian McKaye’s hardcore bite and Glenn Danzig’s full-throated force, with Kevin Iavaroni of New Jersey’s The Shape contributing guest vocals.

Evan Schlomann opens his video with Stallings standing stoically, his glasses shadowed, hands clasped, and face starkly lit against a black background. The shot holds for nearly half a minute before the bright neck of a guitar cuts across the frame. Then the images start to overlap. A second face appears behind the first, and late in the clip the guitar crosses the singer’s chest even as both hands go to his head. There’s a particular unease to watching one person become several while the song asks what’s going to happen to all of us.
Watch the video for Modern Rot below:

Stallings and Schlomann formed Rose Chamber in 2024 after the end of a crossover band, drawing on their shared interest in darkwave and synth music. They come out of hardcore, punk, and metal, with Sentinel in their past and Wretched Rite , Eliminators , and Mutually Assured Destruction among their current bands.

Raven Records issued the duo’s first cassette, State of Affairs , in early 2024. A year later, they shared the Double Feature split tape with The Shape on Death Eternal. My Silhouette brings together the material from both tapes with six new tracks.

My Silhouette (AV!106) is out January 22, 2027 via Avant! Records , with a U.S. co-release from Phage Tapes . The album will be available digitally and on neon-green vinyl in a run of 300 LPs, each with a lyric insert. Pre-order or pre-save the album here.

FILE - Music group Duran Duran poses at The Sony Club in New York, Oct. 12, 2004. From left are John Taylor, Nick Rhodes, Roger Taylor, Simon Le Bon and Andy Taylor.

Andy Taylor, the original guitarist of the 1980s English new wave band Duran Duran, whose huge pop hits included "Hungry Like the Wolf," "The Reflex" and "Rio" and were inextricably linked to the launch of MTV, has died. He was 65.
Taylor's death was confirmed by his family and bandmates in a statement posted on social media and Duran Duran's website.

"From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music. His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental, no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed," the band said.
FILE - Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor listens as a fellow band member answers a question at a news conference in Hong Kong, Aug. 26, 2004.

On the night he was inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in November 2022, Taylor revealed that he had been battling Stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer for several years and was unable to attend.
"I would like to thank each of my brothers in this great band," he wrote. "You can dream about what happened to us but to experience it, on one's own terms, as mates, was beyond incredible."

The two-time Grammy Award-winners had nine gold records and six platinum ones, with 20 Top 20 singles in the U.K. and 18 in the U.S. They were two-time Ivor Novello Award winners and are MTV Video Visionary Award recipients.

The band's 1981 debut album "Duran Duran" had their first hit single, "Planet Earth," but it was "Rio" that transformed them into trans-Atlantic stars. The Rock Hall explained their appeal this way: "They were new wave outsiders who became music video stars — 'Tiger Beat' fashion pinups who rocked arenas."
How music videos made Duran Duran massively famous

The band's imperial stage occurred with a trio of hit albums between 1981 and 1983, with such dance-floor barnburners as "Girls on Film" and "Union of the Snake" and the moody ballads "The Chauffeur" and "Save a Prayer." Other hits in the coming years included "The Wild Boys," "New Moon on Monday" and "Come Undone." Their popularity was cemented when they recorded the James Bond theme song "A View to a Kill" and earned a slot at Live Aid in 1985.

Mixing fashion, pioneering synthesizers and glam-pop swagger, the telegenic band were all over radio and young people's walls, with bassist John Taylor and singer Simon Le Bon becoming heartthrobs and the band being labeled part of the New Romantics. Princess Diana was known to be a fan, which meant a lot to the band.

"It worked well for us," drummer Roger Taylor told Rolling Stone. "It was genuine. I don't think it was some sort of PR stunt. It was massive for us because she was the No. 1 icon of the early '80s."

The band's success was in large part due to their videos, including their Antigua-set song "Rio," which featured shots of the band in pastel suits sailing confidently on a yacht. For the album "Rio," they shot three music videos in Sri Lanka — including "Save a Prayer," which had John Taylor getting sprayed by an elephant — and two in Antigua, feeding MTV's need to have a stream of visuals, something classic rock didn't have.

"A lot of the success of the album is down to the power of the videos and the way it made the band omnipresent around the globe," Le Bon told The Daily Beast in 2012. Andy Taylor agreed: "I don't think we could have done it without MTV."

John Taylor and keyboardist Nick Rhodes started the band as teenagers in the northern city of Birmingham in 1978, with a name inspired by a character in the Jane Fonda-starring sci-fi movie "Barbarella." Duran Duran Guitarist Andy Taylor Has Passed Away at 65
Andy Taylor, the guitarist and co-writer who gave Duran Duran’s early records their bite, died on Monday, November 23, at 65.

Andy Taylor , the guitarist and co-writer who gave Duran Duran ’s early records their bite, died on Monday, November 23, at 65. His family and former bandmates announced on Wednesday that he died at home with his family beside him after a long illness with prostate cancer.

Taylor’s wife, Tracey, remembered a husband, father and grandfather who was happiest when the family was together. She said, “For all the incredible experiences music brought him, family always came first.” She recalled his determination to keep enjoying life through his illness and thanked fans for the comfort their support brought him. The family took comfort in knowing he felt loved.

Simon Le Bon, John Taylor, Nick Rhodes and Roger Taylor recalled the confidence Taylor brought with him to Birmingham and the dry humor that kept them grounded as the band took off. “His playing drove the songs that took us around the world,” they wrote. They said getting to play together again in the early 2000s meant a great deal to them. His letter at the 2022 Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction reminded them how close they still were.
Read the full statement and the band members’ individual tributes here.

Born February 16, 1961, Taylor grew up in Cullercoats on England’s northeast coast. He played working men’s clubs around Newcastle in his teens and had already toured Europe by the time he answered Duran Duran’s Melody Maker ad in 1980. He moved to Birmingham, and that July the classic five-piece played its first gig together at the Rum Runner, the nightclub where they rehearsed.

Taylor co-wrote and played on 1981’s Duran Duran , 1982’s Rio and 1983’s Seven and the Ragged Tiger . His clipped chords on “Girls on Film” leave John Taylor’s bass room to dart around them. “Careless Memories” has the impatient scrape of a band still within earshot of punk. On “Hungry Like the Wolf,” Taylor’s riff is as easy to hum as the chorus.

Andy and John Taylor formed the Power Station with singer Robert Palmer and Chic drummer Tony Thompson. On their 1985 debut, Andy’s heavy guitar chords and Thompson’s outsized drums drove “Some Like It Hot” and a cover of T. Rex’s “Get It On.” Taylor played with both bands at Live Aid in Philadelphia that July. He left Duran Duran in 1986 and released his solo debut, Thunder , the following year. He also played on Palmer’s “Addicted to Love” and co-produced Rod Stewart’s Out of Order .

The classic Duran Duran lineup reunited in 2001 and returned to the stage in 2003. They released Astronaut in 2004, their first studio album together since Seven and the Ragged Tiger . Taylor left again in 2006.

When Duran Duran entered the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2022, illness kept Taylor from the ceremony. Le Bon read from Taylor’s letter disclosing his diagnosis of stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer. The following year, Taylor played alongside Nile Rodgers on “Black Moonlight,” from Duran Duran’s Danse Macabre , and released a solo album, Man’s a Wolf to Man .

Taylor is survived by his wife, Tracey, their children Georgina, Isabella, Bethany and Andrew, and his grandson Albie. His former bandmates asked people to respect the family’s privacy. In lieu of flowers, the family has asked for donations in his memory to Prostate Cancer UK .

What should a festival line-up look like in 2026?
It can be a roll of the dice as to whether a line-up is to your taste or not. Emma Wilkes investigates the changing tides of festival line-ups, from the mainstream to the obscure.

The nights are long, the year is ending, and the once-yellowing grass is now carpeted with frost, but next summer is already taking shape. Every day, it seems, there’s another fresh festival line-up threatening to knock some digits off your bank balance. I should know – I spend this time of year writing news stories about them.

If you’re a regular festival goer, or even if there’s just one particular event you count down the days to return to, it’s a time of year that can bring bated breath and crossed fingers. It can be a roll of the dice as to whether a line-up is to your taste or not. Just like music itself, it’s subjective, and there can be a difference between a festival line-up that’s not to your taste and a line-up that’s an all-round failed throw.

In the last week, I’ve seen the internet split down the middle over two line-ups in particular. This year’s Manchester edition of Outbreak Festival was the most diverse yet controversial in its 15-year history, featuring “The Hayley Williams Show” headlining for two nights on the bounce and a line-up co-curated by Hayley Williams itself, with fewer traditional hardcore acts and wider-spanning alternative names including Wednesday, American Football and Julien Baker. Some were instantly hooked, others – especially Outbreak’s more traditional fans – feeling like the festival had changed beyond recognition.

A couple of days later, Glastonbury unveiled its line-up poster some months earlier than expected. It had the youngest headliners this side of the millennium, in the form of 33-year-old Sam Fender and Harry Styles and 25-year-old returning headliner Billie Eilish, while the rest of the bill leaned younger and more pop-heavy. The Instagram comments paint a divided picture, especially among older Glasto-goers feeling pushed out, or guitar fans feeling it was all a little anaemic with a limited offering for their tastes.

Neither of these are ‘bad’ bills, per se. The Outbreak line-up I love, and the Glasto line-up I appreciate but am relatively unmoved by. But viewed through a lens of objectivity rather than subjectivity, what makes a ‘good’ festival bill?

The crucial question is what a festival is for. Sure, it’s a weekend to dance with your friends, explore music, tick off bucket list bands and fill your head with memories, but every festival poster is a statement. What matters in music right now? Who do people want to see? It should hold up a mirror to what culture looks like, which obviously has commercial purposes as a means to promote an album, but there’s an element of artistic value to it too.

The relevant question to ask could be ‘Is it current?’, but not all festivals necessarily operate with that energy, so perhaps the better one is, ‘Is it relevant?’ Are you booking bands that feel of the moment, whether they’re breaking out or surging back into fashion, or milking the nostalgia cash cow?

Equally important is variety. What’s the use of booking the same bands that do the rounds every year, or the same sort of sounds? There’s an element of curation involved. What sort of vibe is the day going to have? How much choice is there of who to see at a particular time? And it goes without saying - if it’s mostly male and pale from top to bottom, it loses relevancy points. There’s something deeply retrograde about not taking heed of the genuinely meaningful calls for more people to see artists who look like them on festival stages.

There’s also an aspect of cultural responsibility too. The smaller stages of a festival can offer formative experiences for the heroes of the future to draw new fans in and develop how they perform. Festivals need to make the space to nurture that talent, especially those coming up through the grassroots. It’s why it felt like such a disappointment to see Reading and Leeds cut the BBC Introducing stage, and pad out its replacement stage, The Canopy, with nepo babies who may not need the boost. By contrast, the Cheltenham-based 2000trees has always been brilliant at building up new bands, booking them year after year, and creating a culture of what’s known as ‘Trees bands’ who the fans love just as much as they love the festival.

What do 35 years of touring the UK look like to Manic Street Preachers?
Here’s what Nicky Wire remembers best, as told to The Quietus editor John Doran. An excerpt from issue one of SHOWNOTES.

I am very much a homebird, so when it came time for Manic Street Preachers to go on tour I was nervous about it. My Dad had an old grandad’s chair, which he managed to tie to the wall in the back of the hire van, so someone could have a seat on the way to the gig. It was incredibly dangerous. And then on the way back, James would just get in a sleeping bag and lie down in the back of the van, rolling around all over the place as we were driving back home. He can sleep anywhere.

We had such a deep bonding experience on the Motown Junk Tour in 1991. The staff at the venues were just so friendly; you felt that they really cared. I remember getting to the Stoke Wheatsheaf – a magical venue – and we hadn’t had any food for a day and a half. They made us the most beautiful burger and chips.

King Tut’s Wah Wah Hut, Glasgow? The Stoker, Coventry? The Barrel Organ, Birmingham? JB’s, Dudley? Moles, Bath? The Adelphi, Hull? The Leadmill, Sheffield? It was a truly magical tour, I can’t even remember any bad shows.

The greatest one was probably The Buzz Club in Aldershot. What a fucking venue. Who’d have thought if you were in a rock band, going to Aldershot would give you one of the greatest gigs of your life? It was full of squaddies because it’s an army town, and it was antagonistic, but also brilliant. That was on the edge but some gigs could tip over the edge.

We did quite a scary gig at Reading’s After Dark Club. There was a proper firm of football hooligans there. That film The Firm had just been on TV and I don’t know if it had got people excited but it kicked off. James got punched but we stood our ground. There was a real adrenaline rush to it, even if there was a hint of violence at a lot of those early gigs.

What strikes me now is that all of these places were towns and I wonder how many of them have that kind of gig venue left. You can still play gigs in the cities, but to play in these towns was amazing: learning your trade and meeting people. Also realising there are people like you in every town you go to.

Very early doors, Little Chefs were different – they deserve an honourable mention because you could just get a proper meal there. A plate of bacon, egg and chips. Last night marked the end of my birthday week, because spending last week in Paris wasn’t enough- I had to extend it. What a gig to wrap it up with! I’ve been waiting to see C.O.F.F.I.N for…

Last night marked the end of my birthday week, because spending last week in Paris wasn’t enough- I had to extend it. What a gig to wrap it up with! I’ve been waiting to see C.O.F.F.I.N for what has felt like a lifetime, and last night- I finally got to see them. What made it even more special was having Gold Cup as the support.

I’ve seen Gold Cup live this year about 4 times now, and they just keep getting better and better. Despite a few technical issues at the start, they played their set as if they were the headliners. And to be honest, it won’t be long until they are headlining the Pink Room at YES. Some bands are made to be heard live, and Gold Cup are one of those bands. There’s something about their live shows that just makes you feel good and glad to be alive, y’know? I can’t wait for their debut record to come out because it’s just going to make their shows even more wild. They’re the best at what they do, and it felt like the crowd were an even split of Gold Cup and C.O.F.F.I.N fans, and you cannot help but be proud of that. The energy they have on stage and the way they play together is a thing of beauty- and yes, you will leave feeling like you want to start a band because of them.

C.O.F.F.I.N time! Where on earth do I begin? Opening the set with Out In Oslo caused the room to erupt and it pretty much stayed like that for the whole time. Part of me was watching the band, the other part was just obsessed with the crowd. It is so easy to feel unsafe at shows especially when it’s rowdy, but this felt safe. It felt like a community. And as a visibly queer person, that feeling is rare to find right now given how shit the world is. But when you find that safety net, you hold onto it. I love everything that C.O.F.F.I.N stand for, and whilst the night was ridiculously fun- they used their platform to highlight the domestic violence rates in Australia, how corrupt governments are, calling people out on their shitty behaviours and not make life harder for those of us in marginalised communities. Life is tough enough already- just be kind to each other. It’s not hard.

Every song is yelled back at the band, and there are countless stage dives and crowd surfs. You could feel the love for the band in the room, truly. And the sense of being free and being able to express yourself however you want is also felt, and that’s something we should never take for granted. You can tell that the band not only love the bones of each other but they absolutely love playing shows, and you could feel how much it meant to them. I spent the time in awe of Ben because anyone who can sing AND drum at the same time is someone to admire (within reason because there are some people who can do it but y’know…)

Every song is greeted with people in the front throwing their sweaty bodies into each other and having the time of their lives. Some of them may be feeling it today but who cares! The joy on their faces, arms around their mates and strangers- it was so lovely to see because the world is unkind, but that energy did not step foot into the room once last night. What C.O.F.F.I.N have created with their music and live shows is a safe space, and that’s something to really hold onto. For me songs like Fast Love (this was my favourite and it was a tough call) and Give Me A Bite were WILD! Think Bad absolutely ripped too as did White Dog.

You really, really felt the love for the band when they left and everyone demanded an encore (and we got it!) They’re a band that you cannot help but love, and if you’ve not seen the documentary they recently put out- please go to YouTube and find it (it may still be there hopefully.) Not only will you too fall in love with the band and all they stand for, but you’ll just be in awe of their work ethic and how dedicated they are.

C.O.F.F.I.N are for everyone, and their live shows really make you feel it, and their live shows make you appreciate the band even more. I don’t know when they’ll be back in the UK but for now, I will hold onto this show as being one of the best things I’ve seen this year.

The very British problem of GB Music Radio
GB News has launched an all-British radio station. As nationalistic thinkers so often do, they've oversimplified what it means to be British, and diluted the quality of their output in the…

How do you find common ground between a Guardian reader and a Daily Mail reader? Get them talking about British music. Somewhere down the line, they’ll share some musical common ground, or at least bond over their reverence – despite said reverence likely coming from different places – of the factory of musical greatness that is this strange little island.

For the right wing, perhaps it’s a beacon of what makes Great Britain greater than anywhere else. For the left, our music and culture might be the one thing about this country they can feel proud of in an era of decaying support structures and rampant division.

There’s something ironic, then, about right-wing slop spewers GB News positioning their new all-British radio station as a source of unity. Upon its announcement last month, Chief Revenue Officer Ross Sergeant said: “GB Music Radio gives advertisers something genuinely new: a station built around a single, warm idea that almost everyone in this country can get behind.”

Music should be the great unifier. Can a radio station really do that, though, when it’s had red, white and blue vomited all over it courtesy of arguably the most polarising, untrustworthy and hateful news brand in the country? It’s doubtful. For that reason alone, plenty of people wouldn’t touch it with a bargepole.

In fact, something about its announcement felt ridiculous enough to be satirical, especially with how it positioned its show names, like ‘Great British Drive Home’ and ‘Great British Breakfast’. So this is a station for people who chant ‘Come on Ingerland’ as they wolf down their bacon sarnies in the morning before sitting in their very Bri’ish traffic jam (in a vehicle that is decidedly not British)?

Sergeant added: “British music is a shared passion that cuts across generations, and we look forward to helping brands become part of the soundtrack to our listeners' day, from Breakfast with Paul [Coyte] to weekend mornings with Nana [Akua].” Coyte and Akua are already established names on GB News, the former presenting sports shows before pivoting back to music, while Akua recently went viral for a heated exchange with a guest on a panel last month.

Consequently, 'All British, all day’ once again spits in the face of any sort of unity. There’s no hiding the nationalism behind it, as it turns music into a cultural battleground it has dominance over, wresting it out of progressive hands into something it can call its own.

The arts and culture sectors, particularly music, are overwhelmingly left-wing , and music has for decades been a site of community building and changemaking, from Seventies punk values to recent calls for boycotts and solidarity with Palestine.
More recently, when the right have wanted a piece of this, they’ve even turned to AI-generated figureheads such as Danny Bones, who we investigated on the podcast.

GB Music Radio’s other problem is it tries to make the idea of Britishness far more simple and far less nuanced than it is in reality. Who gets to be considered British? What about mixed-nationality artists? Does AI count?

A spokesperson tells Drowned in Sound: “We celebrate British music in the broadest possible sense. British artists, or groups who are British or have British members. For example we will feature Fleetwood Mac. GB Music already features AI generated content in our hourly traffic AI reports but there are no plans for any fully AI songs."

It’s better that it’s broad, of course. To strip away all but the most ‘purely’ British artists certainly leaves the pool looking about as bland and beige as a plate of potato smileys sans sauce. Looking at what they've played at the time of writing, the playlist includes Lewis Capaldi's 'Survive', Pulp's 'Disco 2000' Kajagoogoo's 'Too Shy', Rainbow's 'Since You've Been Gone', David Bowie and Queen's 'Under Pressure' and Duffy's 'Mercy.' These are all songs you could hear if you whacked on Heart, Virgin Radio and the like. It's not all that different from a lot of middle-of-the-road mainstream radio, except without the variety an all-nationality playlist could offer.
Last Tuesday I went to Paris for my birthday. I came home yesterday, and I miss it. I miss friendliness, everything feeling slower, good vegan food, sleeping in a bed that doesn’t hurt my…

Last Tuesday I went to Paris for my birthday. I came home yesterday, and I miss it. I miss friendliness, everything feeling slower, good vegan food, sleeping in a bed that doesn’t hurt my back and a decent shower. It was the perfect way to see off my 30s, and the last band I saw of my 30s on the day before my birthday was Penelope Isles.

What made the show special is that Lily, Jack and I are from the Isle of Man. I felt like a piece of home was in the room on Wednesday night and there were times where I was trying to not cry a little. It’s weird because I have such a weird relationship with the Isle of Man, but that’s not for here. That’s for elsewhere.

I’ve only been to gigs in the UK but I can honestly say that the crowd at Supersonic were just lovely, and it was a joy to be in such a beautiful environment. People were respectful of personal space and there were no drunken idiots ruining it for everyone. Although the set was just under an hour; it was a perfect set. Every song was delivered in such a perfect and tender way. You felt every song, and connected with every word. The set opened with 3, and it was straight into Thinking Seat which just hits you right in the soul and all feels okay. For me, it was Birthdays that did it. That song very nearly got tears out of me (it’s been a comfort) and to see it live was such a gorgeous moment, and it makes you appreciate the song and the record in general, even more so when you see it live. Another Kind Of Love shows just how delicate Jack’s vocals are, and where there are moments in the set where Jack, Lily and Joe absolutely tear the roof off the venue (especially during Gnarbone, which was an insane way to end the show)- you just really see how bloody talented this band is, and they truly deserve the world.

The room felt like it was filled with love and just appreciation for the band, and maybe it was extra special because it was the last night of the tour, but it just felt like one of those shows that people will talk about in years to come and those of us who were there will know exactly how lucky we were. It was a truly stunning show, and is up there as being one of my favourites of the year. Lily, Jack and Joe are just exceptional musicians, and it was a real honour to witness their greatness last week. I also felt super proud that a band from where I’m from are playing venues like Supersonic and just being a dream to watch.

At the end of the show, my partner and I went up to the merch stand and Lily spotted my Bushy’s t-shirt. I told her I was from the Isle of Man, and it was one of the most wholesome moments I’ve had. Jack and I had our photo taken together, with our Bushy’s shirts, and spoke about home for a little bit. It was nice to have a piece of home and to meet the band who have again, released one of the best records of the year.

If you’ve not listened to 3 yet, I urge you to do so. There is so much love, loss, thought, care and heart on the record and when you witness it live- you hear the record differently. The bond between Jack and Lily is so beautiful, and you just feel so lucky to witness the greatness of all 3 of them on stage together. At times the songs are mellow and soothing, and there are other moments in the set where this gorgeous loudness takes over. Ending the set with Gnarbone was just heaven! Opening or closing with it was always going to be magic!

Another Kind Of Love going into Birthdays then into Moonwalker was a piece of musical heaven. I honestly couldn’t have wished for a better band to say bye bye to my 30s to (I saw Fontaines D.C the day after my birthday on Friday, so I really have lucked out here!)
It’s pretty fair to say that Penny Isles show is truly special, and you take what you need from it. It’ll make you wish you could watch them every night in Paris. Everything is better in Paris.
(There’s another cool photo of us on the Penny Isles Instagram too!)

I should be packing for my birthday trip to Paris tomorrow, but I feel I need to write about the new PINS single. The last thing I’ll write in my 30s. What way to say goodbye to my 30s than to write about a band that I love a hell of a lot, and who’s music has got me through most of my 30s and the latter part of my 20s.

The new single by PINS, No More Tears is beautiful. And if you want to truly feel the beauty of the song and soak up the vulnerability of the lyrics- then watch the music videos. PINS have always made stunning music videos, but the one for No More Tears has a real sense of community, love, friendship, some loss, healing, and honesty. No More Tears is a real tender moment, and it almost feels like a lullaby. Maybe it is. Maybe it’s a lullaby with added bite. Honestly, this is PINS at their very best. It’s such a dreamy, blissed-out song with their signature touch; how could you not become obsessed with this gem of a song! I will talk about this band (and many others) to anyone who will listen, and I think this could be my go to PINS song if someone hasn’t heard them before. Start with this, and prepare to have your mind blown and your heart stolen.

I say it every single time, but that’s because PINS are consistently great, however this again just shows how fantastic the band are. Lyrically, musically, vocally- everything. The video is dedicated to their friend Em, and adding something so precious to the end of the video makes you appreciate the song even more. Grief is a thief and we face it however and whatever way we can. Thank goodness we have music. Will I cry when they do this live? Of course. I cry too much, ha!

No More Tears has no resemblance to any thing PINS have done before but fits perfectly in with the songs they’ve released from the new record to date, and I think that’s pretty much setting us up for a strong contender for the best record of 2027. I cannot wait for the new record, and they are playing some special shows to coincide with the release. I’ve seen them nearing 20 odd times I think now, and this will be my first time seeing them in Manchester. I have no idea how it’s taken me so long, but I cannot wait.

Slapping someone in the face is now a sport. Yes, I’m surprised too. The rules are straightforward. Competitors stand either side of a central podium. In each round, they are permitted to strike their opponent – open-handed, ungloved, cheek only – a single time. After one minute of recovery time, they must allow themselves to be struck back. Bouts range between three and five rounds. Victory can be earned on points – the three judges look for clean technique and the impact a strike makes – but about half are won via knockout. The podium is padded, as the competitors sometimes collide with it on the way down. Behind each competitor stand two catchers to grab them as they fall. When Power Slap introduced a super-heavyweight division, where contestants can weigh the same as an upright piano, they hired professional strongmen for the job.

This Is the Best Christmas Movie for You, According to Your Zodiac Sign
Yes, holiday magic exists—and we have the proof right here, with the perfect Christmas movie for you.

There’s an eternal debate swirling around whether Die Hard is actually a Christmas movie, but you know the answer, Aries. You love a good fight, and you will happily present your detailed, 10-point argument to anyone who will listen. Heck, you’d watch this flick just because of the debate behind it. Though, let’s be honest, as a sign ruled by war-driven Mars, you really love the idea of mixing a beloved, sedate holiday with an impromptu hostage takeover.

Another reason you’ll gravitate toward this one? You tend to operate under main-character energy, so you’ll relate to the fact that John McClane stumbles into the middle of a terrorist plot and is somehow the only one who can help. That would totally be you, Aries, and now you’re locked in. Bonus: Because it’s packed with nonstop action , you won’t have time to get bored. Yes, we know you only make it through half of most Christmas movies before jumping to the next thing. Yippee-ki-yay—yeah, we’re not going to finish that phrase. It’s Christmas!

You’re all about maintaining tradition , Taurus; it’s one of the things that makes you the most stubborn sign out there. It’s also why Clark’s unwavering commitment to the perfect Christmas in Christmas Vacation is so classically you. The lights will work, the family will gather and this will be a Christmas to remember! And that moment when Clark devolves into destitute mania after opening that envelope from his boss will totally resonate with you. More than 200,000 Carbon Monoxide Detectors Are Being Recalled Due to the Risk of “Serious Injury or…
Around 210,000 carbon monoxide detectors are being recalled because they don't properly detect dangerous levels of carbon monoxide.

Some recalls are more serious than others, and this is a serious one. More than 210,000 carbon monoxide and natural gas detectors are being recalled because they can fail to alert consumers to dangerous levels of carbon monoxide , potentially putting people at risk of serious injury or death.
The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) announced the recall on Wednesday, Nov. 25, involving Steadfast Haven 4-in-1 plug-in CO and natural gas detectors sold by Zenara Commerce LLC.
What consumers need to know about the recall
So, how do you know if you have an affected device? Here’s the scoop.

The recall covers models KH158 and GC03, with approximately 210,410 units affected. The KH158 model is round in shape. It comes in gray or white plastic housing with a black digital display. Meanwhile, the GC03 model is rectangular with a black housing and a black digital display. Consumers can find the model number on the white label on the back of the device, right near the plug.
Consumers purchased the detectors online at Truststeadfast.com between February 2026 and September 2026. They cost around $48 to $70.

The biggest concern is that these devices may not sound an alarm when hazardous levels of carbon monoxide are present. Carbon monoxide is particularly dangerous because it is odorless and colorless, making a functioning detector an important safety device in the home.
According to the CPSC, Zenara has received one report of a detector failing to alarm during a carbon monoxide leak. No injuries have been reported, however.

Consumers should contact Zenara immediately to request a free replacement. The company is asking customers to register at www.truststeadfast.com/pages/recall , mark the recalled detector with the word “RECALLED” and their initials using permanent marker, then upload a photo of the marked product.
Consumers should continue using their recalled detectors until the replacement is installed. Once registration is confirmed, they should dispose of the recalled unit in their household trash.

For additional information, consumers can email recall@truststeadfast.com or visit the company’s recall website. Given the potential consequences, this is one recall homeowners won’t want to overlook.

12 Common Holiday-Party Disasters—And How to Fix Them ASAP
From kitchen mishaps to awkward moments with guests, even the most carefully planned celebration can go awry. Here's how to keep your cool and save the day.

I entertain a lot around the holidays, and I mean a lot: an annual party with former work colleagues; a Hanukkah dinner (I’m not Jewish, but my crew love latkes); a homemade-pizza night and gingerbread-house-building session with my niece, her BFF and their moms; and, of course, the Feast of the Seven Fishes, the Italian American Christmas Eve tradition .

I’m a planner, and an incredibly organized one, at that. I’ve got spreadsheets with shopping lists, ingredient lists, detailed to-do lists … you get the picture. And yet, no matter how prepared I am, things happen. Like the time I dropped a baking dish of perfectly browned, crispy-edged roasted potatoes on my tile floor, or the time—or, should I say, times?—I ran out of ice. Because here’s the thing: Holiday-party disasters are inevitable. You can plan for every possible scenario, but eventually something will go sideways. And when it does, well, the party must go on.

The trick is knowing how to recover without turning a minor snafu into a major production. As event planner Renee Patrone Rhinehart puts it, “Your guests probably have no idea something went wrong until you start announcing it to everyone.” Her advice? “Just roll with it!”

To find out how to roll with a dozen of the most common holiday-party disasters when you’re hosting , I went to the experts. Iron Chef Alex Guarnaschelli and renowned Southern chef Carla Hall weigh in on turkey troubles and other food emergencies; event planners Rhinehart and Marcy Blum share their secrets for keeping a party on track; etiquette expert Myka Meier offers advice for navigating awkward social situations; and licensed marriage and family therapist Nari Jeter, PhD, weighs in on emotionally charged moments.

So whether your turkey is taking forever to cook, an unexpected guest arrives or your uncle decides today is the perfect time to reignite that family feud, here’s how to save the celebration—and your sanity. Party on!

You’re still getting dressed, the kitchen is a disaster zone, and the appetizers aren’t even out yet. Then the doorbell rings—20 minutes before you expected anyone. Now you need to switch into host mode, and fast.

What to do: Welcome them warmly, offer a drink , and, if you’re comfortable, give them a small task, like putting on the music or lighting candles. “You’re early! Perfect timing. Grab a drink, and help me finish up!” is a perfectly acceptable response, says Rhinehart. My friends know that’s the case at my house: You show up early, and I’m putting you to work.

(For what it’s worth: Meier notes that guests should arrive at the stated time for a seated dinner; for a more casual gathering, arriving 10 to 15 minutes after the start time is generally appropriate.)

Why it works: You don’t need to drop everything to entertain an early arrival. A little hospitality goes a long way, and giving someone a simple job can make them feel included rather than in the way. It can even turn into a bonding moment with your new guest!

You planned dinner for eight, set the table for eight and made just enough food for eight. Then someone shows up with an unexpected plus-one. You could panic about the extra chair and plate, or you could get creative and make it work.

What to do: Take a breath , pull up an extra chair and welcome that person as though you expected them all along. “As a host, your goal is to make everyone feel welcome, even when you’re caught off guard,” says Meier. Simply say, “How lovely to meet you! Come on in.” After all, she adds, “It was not the guest’s fault they were asked to be there, and you don’t want them to feel that when arriving.”

Blum says to have card stock and a pen on hand to make an extra place card, if necessary. Rhinehart recommends stretching the meal with whatever you have—bread, salad or an extra side—and resisting the urge to announce that you weren’t prepared for another person.

Why it works: You’re taking charge, being an excellent hostess and rolling with the surprise. Making a fuss, on the other hand, can turn a small logistical hiccup into an awkward moment. As Rhinehart says, “Nobody needs to know!”

Is It Really Rude to Opt Out of the Gift Exchange?
The anxiety—and financial pressure—of getting a present for a group gift swap can feel exhausting during an already overscheduled season. Can you just skip it? The post Is It Really Rude to…

Like all torturous extended family traditions, ours started with good intentions. One year, someone got left off the list during our chaotic annual Christmas gift free-for-all. Feelings were hurt. So being responsible adults, we fixed the problem by inventing an entire bureaucracy: the Official Family Gift Exchange.

The idea was fine. The rules were what ruined us. It started with just drawing names. Then we added a price limit. Then a price minimum, after somebody’s “gift” turned out to be an already-opened bottle of lotion. Then a rule requiring you to talk to your assigned person about their interests, which metastasized into a 15-question survey, then into a shared spreadsheet, tracked with the rigor of a Pentagon budget.

Then the “ no regifting ” clause. Then the Great Gift Card Debate, which raged for years: Do gift cards even count as real gifts? Does one to a specific store outrank a Visa card? Does it have to be taped to something ­wrappable, or are we now just handing each other receipts?

It all came to a head the year my husband’s gift got returned to him. Not regifted— returned, like a defective toaster , with a note that it wasn’t thoughtful enough. Being an eternal optimist, he tried again. That gift also came back, this time via USPS, meaning the recipient paid actual postage to send it away rather than keep it one more day. That’s when we knew we wanted out. It wasn’t working anymore.

My husband and I decided to pull the plug. No elaborate exchange, just a gift card to each family, no survey required. What had started as a fun, generous tradition had somehow turned into a monthlong hostage situation that began every November.

Naturally, quitting had consequences: The following year, someone anonymously (although I’m pretty sure I know who) sent us a calendar of dogs pooping. (Yes, that’s a thing. And yes, you can buy it. I do not recommend gifting it, though I also cannot stop thinking about the person who decided the world needed it as a wall calendar.)

It’s not just my family that has a hard time managing this. More often than not, gift exchanges—office, family or friend group—start as a fun idea but end up being a spreadsheet with hurt feelings. So is opting out of the whole enterprise actually rude?

Financially, gift exchanges have quietly inflated like everything else. A $10 white elephant gag gift is now a $25-and-up “guideline” that creeps to $40 the second someone brings a nice candle. Multiply that by the office exchange, the neighborhood exchange and the family swaps, and you’re out $200 before buying anything for someone you actually live with. And, it must be said, in this economy?

There are also the plain logistics: Exchanges take time most of us don’t have in December. Saying no to one more obligation isn’t a personality flaw; it’s functioning boundaries. And if the group’s response to “I’ll sit this one out” is outrage, that says more about their expectations than your manners.

If only it were that easy. Gift swaps, especially the family and friend kind, aren’t really about the gift. They’re a shared ritual , and rituals only work if everyone shows up. Opt out and you can shift the whole dynamic—an odd number of ornaments, a recalculated spreadsheet, or Grandma noticing the empty spot under the tree and asking about it at dinner, forever.

There’s also the momentum problem. Once one person opts out “just this year,” the tradition can quietly die. If the exchange genuinely matters to the group, your exit—however ­reasonable—can be the beginning of the end for people who looked forward to it.

Context is everything, and office, family and friend exchanges are not all the same animal. Office exchanges are the easiest to skip—it’s a workplace, not a family reunion, and “I’m sitting this one out” needs zero explanation. Unless, of course, your boss makes it mandatory.

In contemplating the theory of general relativity, Albert Einstein imagined a falling lift in which people are performing experiments :

One of the observers takes a handkerchief and a watch from his pocket and drops them. What happens to these two bodies? … [F]or the outside observer they are both falling with the same acceleration. But so is the lift, with its walls, ceiling, and floor. Therefore: the distance between the two bodies and the floor will not change.

This notion of the equivalence between gravity and acceleration, which he called “the happiest thought of my life,” came to Einstein in 1907. Interestingly, Lewis Carroll had explored a similar scenario in 1889:
‘One can easily imagine a situation,’ said Arthur, ‘where things would necessarily have no weight, relatively to each other, though each would have its usual weight, looked at by itself.’
‘Some desperate paradox!’ said the Earl. ‘Tell us how it could be. We shall never guess it.’
‘Well, suppose this house, just as it is, placed a few billion miles above a planet, and with nothing else near enough to disturb it: of course it falls to the planet?’
The Earl nodded. ‘Of course — though it might take some centuries to do it.’
‘And is five-o’clock-tea to be going on all the while?’ said Lady Muriel.

‘That, and other things,’ said Arthur. ‘The inhabitants would live their lives, grow up and die, and still the house would be falling, falling, falling! But now as to the relative weight of things. Here’s How to Easily Record Your Entire Family History So No One Forgets Who’s Who in All Those Photos
Up to your eyeballs in old photos, letters and records? These expert tips to document your family history will help you organize everything and connect the dots.

My sister and I were recently hanging out at her place, and the conversation turned to our childhood. I pulled up some old photos on my phone—snaps of pictures that used to live in albums at the center of my parents’ living room. We started taking guesses about when they were from and shared stories about what was happening in them. We both remembered family picnics at the waterfall, our dog Cujo (yes, Cujo), and flying kites in the cornfield across the house. But there were people, places and stories I couldn’t recall at all, like a close family friend’s house we spent a lot of time at; my sister could still describe it in detail.
That’s when it hit me: It had been years since we’d flipped through old albums like that. As physical albums get left behind and older relatives depart, we’re increasingly losing our family history.

I’ve researched bits of my family’s genealogy over the years, but I’ve always run into roadblocks. Like many families in the U.S., our ancestors immigrated several generations ago, and a lot of details were lost or changed along the way. How do you document family history when there are so many missing pieces? By tackling it little by little, says Allison Singleton, the genealogy services manager at the Genealogy Center. “There will be gaps of information you don’t know,” she says. But don’t let that stop you.

That being said, you’ll have a lot more luck if you have a method to the madness. That’s why I reached out to a few experts who do this for a living and could lay it out in simple terms for us. In addition to Singleton, I spoke with Kyle Betit, a senior genealogist at Ancestry; Haleh Shoa, a certified professional photo organizer and the founder of Picturli; and Peter Andrew Wint, the founder of Family Roots.

It turns out, there are a lot of strategies and resources available, and some of them are free. Read on to find out how to document family history , create a family tree and be the detective your clan needs—starting now!
How on earth do you even start this kind of project?
Before you dive into documenting your family’s history, determine your goal. “Knowing where you want to end up tells you where to start and how much you need to gather,” Shoa says.

Next, collect supplies. Shoa says you’ll need several plastic bins, colorful index cards for categorizing batches of photos, an archival pencil, a 2TB or 4TB external hard drive for storage, nitrile gloves for handling photos, and a notebook or spreadsheet for tracking.

Then, gather the documentation you already have and group it into categories. Think of this like taking an inventory. “Put like with like,” Shoa says. “The albums, the slides, the negatives and the VHS tapes should each have their own piles.” In addition to photos and videos, include things like old letters , newspaper clippings, obituaries, birth and death certificates, and recipe cards. “These items are full of clues about your family history,” Singleton notes. After you’ve grouped everything, you’ll dig into each category. (More on that below.)

Keep in mind that you don’t need to do everything at once. “Start small—with one photograph, one document, one family story, one person or one question—and see how your research progresses,” Singleton advises. After all, you don’t want to get overwhelmed before you even really start!
How do you create a family tree?
To create a family tree, gather and cross-check details about your family, and designate a place to keep it all organized. Follow these steps to get started.
Building your tree online allows you to save and share it virtually, and on some platforms, you can turn on collaborative permissions so relatives can contribute in real time.

If you’re looking for a free and simple platform that’s particularly good for beginners, Shoa recommends Family Echo. You can also create a basic free tree in FamilySearch, Canva, Ancestry and MyHeritage. Just be aware that free trees may have limitations, and access to some records and services may require a paid subscription.
